_rules.backslash_escaping: Every LaTeX backslash is doubled in JSON. Write \\sigma to render \sigma. Matrix row breaks become \\\\.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A risk analyst at an equity derivatives desk is presenting to a group of newly hired analysts and wants to define the volatility smile precisely. Which of the following best defines a volatility smile?

options.text: The plot of an option's historical volatility, measured across successive trading days, for a series of options with different expiration dates.
The plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.
The plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given strike price, as a function of its time to maturity.
The plot of the market price of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the two axes of the smile, and how implied volatility varies as the strike parameter varies while maturity is held fixed.

Implied volatility is the volatility input that, when fed into Black-Scholes-Merton, returns a model price exactly equal to the observed traded price:

$$c(S, K, \sigma_{implied}, r, q, T) = c_{\text{market}}$$

There is no closed-form solution; it is found by iteration, and because vega is strictly positive the solution is unique. The three related plots differ only in which parameter is varied and which is held fixed:

| Plot | Y-axis | X-axis varies | Held fixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volatility smile | Implied volatility | Strike $K$ | Maturity $T$ |
| Volatility term structure | Implied volatility | Maturity $T$ | Strike $K$ |
| Volatility surface | Implied volatility | Both $K$ and $T$ | Nothing |

A volatility skew is the name given to a smile that is not symmetric, which in practice means any smile that is not flat.

a.reason: Historical volatility is backward looking and estimated from past returns, while the smile uses forward-looking implied volatility backed out of traded prices. The option also varies the wrong parameter: trading days and expirations rather than strikes.

b.reason: Implied volatility on the vertical axis, strike on the horizontal axis, maturity held fixed.

c.reason: This is the volatility term structure. It holds strike fixed and varies maturity, which is exactly the reverse of the smile.

d.reason: Plotting price against strike gives the option price curve, which for calls is monotonically decreasing. The smile plots the volatility implied by those prices, not the prices themselves. This confuses the observable with the quantity inferred from it.

trap.explanation: Option (c) confuses the smile with the term structure, the highest-frequency definitional error in this material, since both plot implied volatility but against opposite axes. Option (a) confuses forward-looking implied volatility with backward-looking historical volatility. Option (d) widens the y-axis from a volatility to a price. The discipline is to name both axes before agreeing with any definition.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew | Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A junior analyst claims that the classic Black-Scholes-Merton framework, which assumes geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility, "produces a volatility smile." Which implied volatility shape is in fact the one consistent with the lognormal price distribution assumed by BSM?

options.text: A symmetric smile, because heavy tails are a feature of the lognormal distribution.
A downward-sloping skew, because the lognormal distribution is positively skewed.
A flat, horizontal line, because a single constant volatility prices every strike correctly.
An inverted smile, or frown, because the lognormal distribution has thinner tails than the normal distribution.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the flat smile as the null hypothesis implied by the model. Any curvature is evidence the market rejects the distributional assumption.

BSM assumes constant volatility and a lognormal terminal price, equivalently normally distributed log returns. If both held exactly, one volatility would price every option correctly regardless of strike, so backing implied volatility out of each traded price would return the same number at every strike. Plotted, that is a horizontal line.

It follows that neither a smile nor a skew is consistent with BSM. Each is a measured departure from it:

| Observed shape | Implied distribution relative to lognormal |
|---|---|
| Flat, horizontal | Lognormal. BSM holds. |
| Symmetric smile | Heavy left tail and heavy right tail |
| Frown, inverted smile | Thin left tail and thin right tail |
| Downward-sloping skew | Heavy left tail, thin right tail. Typical equity pattern. |
| Upward-sloping skew | Thin left tail, heavy right tail |

a.reason: Reverses the benchmark. A smile signals tails heavier than lognormal, so the lognormal cannot itself be the heavy-tailed case; it is the yardstick against which "heavy" is measured.

b.reason: The positive skewness of the lognormal price level is already fully embedded in BSM prices. The observed downward skew is a departure from BSM, indicating a heavier left tail than lognormality permits. The option applies a true property of the lognormal outside the domain where it is relevant.

c.reason: Constant volatility across strikes is precisely what a horizontal implied volatility line means.

d.reason: A frown signals tails thinner than lognormal, which is again a departure from the model rather than a consequence of it.

trap.explanation: Candidates over-drill the fact that equity options display a downward skew and then attribute the skew to the model instead of to the market. The smile exists only because BSM is wrong; if BSM were right there would be nothing to plot. Options (a) and (d) reverse the direction of the departure, one in each tail direction, and option (b) applies a true fact about the lognormal outside the domain where it is relevant.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: Three traders at three different firms observe exactly the same set of traded market prices for European options on the same underlying, with identical strikes and maturity. Each independently computes an implied volatility smile. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: All three must obtain the same smile, because implied volatility is derived from observed market prices and those prices are identical for all three.
All three must obtain the same smile, because put-call parity forces a unique implied volatility at each strike.
The three smiles will coincide only if all three use the same option pricing model, because implied volatility is defined relative to a model.
The three smiles will differ at every strike, because implied volatility cannot be uniquely recovered from an option price.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: implied volatility is a model-dependent parameter, not a market observable. The price is observed; the volatility is inferred through a model.

Implied volatility is defined implicitly as the $\sigma$ solving:

$$\text{Model}(S, K, \sigma, r, q, T) = \text{observed market price}$$

The left side contains a model. Change the model and the $\sigma$ that solves the equation changes, even though the right side has not moved. A trader using a stochastic volatility model and a trader using BSM will back out different numbers from an identical price.

Put-call parity does force the call and put implied volatilities to agree at a given strike and maturity, but only within a single model. It says nothing about agreement across models.

Note also that within a given model the solution is unique, because vega is strictly positive and the model price is therefore strictly increasing in $\sigma$. Uniqueness is not the issue; model choice is.

a.reason: Shared prices are necessary but not sufficient. The mapping from price to volatility runs through a model, which is a free choice made independently by each trader.

b.reason: Hands put-call parity a power it does not have. Parity equates the call and put implied volatilities at a given strike within one model. It does not pin the value down across models.

c.reason: The condition for agreement is a common model, not merely common prices.

d.reason: A claim stated with total certainty that is also technically false. Because vega is strictly positive, implied volatility is uniquely recoverable within any given model. The option confuses the absence of a closed-form solution with the absence of a solution.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is attractive because implied volatility genuinely has no analytical solution and must be found by iteration; no analytical solution is not the same as no unique solution. Option (b) hands put-call parity a cross-model authority it does not possess, when in fact it only equates call and put implied volatility within one model.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on implied volatility
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A trader observes a European call and a European put on the same non-dividend-paying stock. The two options share an identical strike price of USD 60.00 and an identical maturity of six months. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between their implied volatilities?

options.text: The implied volatilities are identical, because put-call parity forces the dollar pricing error of the model to be the same for both options.
The implied volatilities differ, because a put's payoff is bounded above while a call's payoff is unbounded.
The implied volatilities are identical only when both options are at the money.
The implied volatilities are identical only if the underlying price distribution is genuinely lognormal.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: put-call parity implies a single volatility smile, and a single volatility surface, for European calls and European puts.

Put-call parity is a no-arbitrage identity that binds model prices and market prices alike:

$$c_{BSM} + Ke^{-rT} = p_{BSM} + S_0$$
$$c_{market} + Ke^{-rT} = p_{market} + S_0$$

Subtracting the second from the first, the $Ke^{-rT}$ and $S_0$ terms cancel exactly:

$$c_{BSM} - c_{market} = p_{BSM} - p_{market}$$

In words: the dollar pricing error BSM commits on the call is exactly the dollar pricing error it commits on the put. Since the BSM price of each is strictly increasing in volatility, the single volatility that drives the call error to zero must also drive the put error to zero.

Therefore the implied volatility of a European call always equals that of a European put with the same strike and maturity. Extending across all strikes, the smile is shared. Extending across strikes and maturities, the surface is shared. The results also hold to a good approximation for American options.

a.reason: States the mechanism rather than only the conclusion. Equality of dollar pricing errors is what delivers equality of implied volatilities.

b.reason: Payoff asymmetry affects the levels of the two prices, which is why a call and a put at the same strike do not cost the same. It has no bearing on the equality of implied volatilities, which follows from an identity that is silent about payoffs.

c.reason: Narrows a result that holds at every strike to the at-the-money strike alone. Restricting it that way would make the concept of a shared smile meaningless.

d.reason: Imposes a condition the result does not require. Parity is distribution-free. The entire point of the reading is that lognormality fails and yet the call and put smiles still coincide exactly.

trap.explanation: Option (d) catches candidates who reflexively attach the lognormal assumption to every BSM-adjacent result, but put-call parity is a no-arbitrage identity holding under any distribution while the BSM pricing formula is the model requiring lognormality. Options (c) and (d) are both conditions that the true result does not require, one narrowing the strike range and one adding a distributional requirement.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on implied volatility
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: The risk-free rate is 5.0% per annum and a non-dividend-paying stock trades at USD 80.00. The two most liquid options on the stock are a European call and a European put, both struck at USD 70.00 and both maturing in three months. The implied volatility of the call is 30.0% and the implied volatility of the put is 38.0%. Which trade most directly exploits this situation?

options.text: Buy the call, sell the put, and short the stock.
Buy the put, sell the call, and buy the stock.
Buy the call, buy the put, and sell a straddle.
No trade. Different implied volatilities for a call and a put at the same strike and maturity are a normal feature of the volatility surface.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: unequal implied volatilities at a common strike and maturity signal a put-call parity violation, and the arbitrage is executed by buying the cheap option, selling the rich one, and neutralising the resulting synthetic forward.

Step 1. Diagnose. Parity requires the two implied volatilities to be equal. The put carries 38.0% against the call's 30.0%, and price is increasing in implied volatility, so the put is rich and the call is cheap relative to one another.

Step 2. Identify the overpriced side of the parity relation.

$$c + Ke^{-rT} = p + S_0$$

With the put rich, the right-hand portfolio (put plus stock) is worth more in the market than the left-hand portfolio (call plus a bond paying $K$). Sell the expensive portfolio and buy the cheap one: sell the rich side (short the put and short the stock), buy the cheap side (buy the call and lend $Ke^{-rT}$).

That is: buy the call, sell the put, short the stock. Cross-check the structure. Long call plus short put at the same strike is a synthetic long forward carrying full directional exposure. Shorting the stock neutralises it, leaving a locked-in profit with no directional risk, the signature of an arbitrage rather than a bet.

a.reason: Buys the cheap option, sells the rich option, and hedges the synthetic forward the option legs create.

b.reason: The exact reverse trade. It buys the rich put and sells the cheap call, locking in a loss of the same magnitude.

c.reason: Buying a call and a put at the same strike is a long straddle, so selling a straddle at the same strike and maturity cancels the position exactly and leaves nothing but transaction costs. It also fails to isolate the relative mispricing between the two options.

d.reason: Applies to the wrong axis of the surface. Implied volatility does vary across different strikes and different maturities, which is the smile and the term structure. It cannot differ between a call and a put sharing both.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the exact reverse trade and is by far the most commonly selected wrong answer on this template; the fix is a two-step discipline, name which instrument is rich, then confirm the stock leg neutralises the synthetic forward. Option (c) cancels the very position it should be building. Option (d) applies correct language about the surface to the one dimension where it does not hold.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question:
A colleague asserts that equity prices and equity volatility are empirically negatively correlated. The table below shows BSM model prices computed with a constant volatility of 30.0% alongside observed market prices for European options on a stock trading at USD 60.00. All options have six months to maturity and the risk-free rate is 5.0% per annum.

| Strike $K$ | $K/S$ | BSM call (30%) | BSM put (30%) | Market call | Market put |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| USD 45.00 | 0.75 | 16.45 | 0.34 | 17.78 | 1.67 |
| USD 50.00 | 0.83 | 12.23 | 0.99 | 13.29 | 2.05 |
| USD 55.00 | 0.92 | 8.63 | 2.27 | 9.19 | 2.83 |
| USD 60.00 | 1.00 | 5.78 | 4.30 | 5.78 | 4.30 |
| USD 65.00 | 1.08 | 3.69 | 7.08 | 3.19 | 6.58 |
| USD 70.00 | 1.17 | 2.25 | 10.52 | 1.53 | 9.80 |
| USD 75.00 | 1.25 | 1.32 | 14.47 | 0.67 | 13.82 |

What is the shape of the implied volatility curve, and is it consistent with the colleague's assertion?

options.text: An upward-sloping skew, and it is consistent with the assertion.
A downward-sloping skew, and it is consistent with the assertion.
A symmetric smile, but it is not consistent with the assertion.
A frown, but it is not consistent with the assertion.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: reading the direction of the implied volatility curve from the sign of the model pricing error across strikes, and linking a downward skew to negative price-volatility correlation.

The shortcut: because vega is strictly positive, implied volatility exceeds 30.0% at any strike where the market price exceeds the BSM price at 30.0%, and falls below 30.0% wherever the market price is lower. No implied volatility need be solved for.

| Strike | Call error (market minus model) | Implied volatility versus 30% |
|---|---|---|
| USD 45.00 | +1.33 | above |
| USD 50.00 | +1.06 | above |
| USD 55.00 | +0.56 | above |
| USD 60.00 | 0.00 | equal |
| USD 65.00 | -0.50 | below |
| USD 70.00 | -0.72 | below |
| USD 75.00 | -0.65 | below |

Implied volatility falls monotonically as strike rises: a downward-sloping skew, the typical equity pattern.

Consistency: negative correlation between price and volatility means a falling stock is a more volatile stock. That stretches the lower tail of the implied distribution relative to lognormal, raising the value and hence the implied volatility of options struck low, which are the out-of-the-money puts and in-the-money calls. Exactly the pattern in the table, so the shape is consistent.

A second cross-check confirming the shared-smile result: the put errors equal the call errors at every strike. At $K=45.00$: $1.67-0.34=1.33=17.78-16.45$. At $K=75.00$: $13.82-14.47=-0.65=0.67-1.32$. One smile serves both instruments.

a.reason: An upward slope requires market prices above model prices at high strikes, the reverse of the table. It would also imply a heavy right tail, corresponding to positive price-volatility correlation, contradicting the assertion.

b.reason: Monotonically falling implied volatility, consistent with the negative correlation claim.

c.reason: A symmetric smile requires positive errors at both ends with errors near zero in the middle. Here the errors change sign once and monotonically. The second clause is also wrong: a symmetric smile is silent about the sign of any correlation.

d.reason: A frown requires negative errors at both ends and a positive error at the money. The table shows the opposite at the low-strike end and a zero error at the money.

trap.explanation: A candidate who tries to back out seven implied volatilities by iteration under time pressure will reach the same answer too slowly; the shortcut is the sign of (market minus model). The content trap is answering only the first half of the question, since options (c) and (d) pair a wrong shape with a "not consistent" verdict that is superficially attractive to anyone who has not verified the correlation direction.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question:
An analyst computes implied volatilities from traded call options on a large-cap technology stock. The resulting skew is typical of equity options: implied volatility is a decreasing function of strike price. She draws four conclusions.

I. The implied distribution has negative skewness and negative excess kurtosis.
II. For identical maturities, an in-the-money call is more expensive than an out-of-the-money put.
III. Compared with the normal distribution, the implied distribution has a lighter left tail.
IV. Compared with the lognormal distribution, the implied distribution has a lighter right tail.

Which of her conclusions is necessarily true?

options.text: IV only
I only
II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Concept tested: precisely what a downward skew does and does not license you to infer about the implied distribution.

Base result: a downward skew means high implied volatility at low strikes and low implied volatility at high strikes. Low strikes price the left tail (out-of-the-money puts, in-the-money calls); high strikes price the right tail. So relative to the lognormal benchmark the implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a lighter right tail.

IV is necessarily true: a direct restatement of the base result, with the correct benchmark (lognormal) and the correct direction (lighter right tail).

I is not necessarily true: one heavy tail and one light tail does not pin down overall excess kurtosis, which measures total tail weight and can come out positive, zero, or negative. Negative excess kurtosis would require both tails to be light, which the skew contradicts on the left.

II is not necessarily true and is misframed: the statement fixes only the maturity, not the strike, so a comparison between an in-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put is undefined. The defensible statement is that at a given strike an in-the-money call is more expensive than an in-the-money put, which follows from parity rather than from the skew.

III is false on two counts: the skew implies a heavier, not lighter, left tail; and the benchmark is the lognormal distribution, not the normal.

a.reason: IV alone is necessarily true.

b.reason: Requires statement I, which overreaches from an observation about one tail to a claim about total kurtosis. The skew constrains the tails asymmetrically and therefore says nothing determinate about their sum.

c.reason: Requires statements II and III. III reverses the tail direction and simultaneously swaps the benchmark from lognormal to normal.

d.reason: Requires I and II in addition to IV. Only IV survives.

trap.explanation: Statement III is the highest-yield distractor: under time pressure the word "lighter" reads as familiar because statement IV also says "lighter", but IV concerns the right tail against the lognormal while III concerns the left tail against the normal, and both differences matter. Statement I is the scope trap: never promote a one-tail observation into a claim about kurtosis.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A quantitative analyst believes that the volatility of a particular asset is uncertain and positively correlated with the asset's price. Relative to prices implied by a constant volatility assumption, which of the following is most plausible?

options.text: Lower prices for out-of-the-money puts and higher prices for in-the-money puts.
Lower prices for out-of-the-money calls and higher prices for in-the-money calls.
Lower prices for at-the-money calls and higher prices for at-the-money puts.
Lower prices for in-the-money puts and higher prices for out-of-the-money puts.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the two-step mapping from a price-volatility correlation assumption, to a tail shape, to relative option prices by strike.

Step 1. Correlation to tails. Positive correlation means high prices come with high volatility and low prices with low volatility. The upper tail is stretched and the lower tail compressed relative to lognormal: a heavier right tail and a lighter left tail. This is the reverse of the equity pattern, which arises from negative correlation.

Step 2. Tails to strikes. Convert moneyness into strike position explicitly:

| Priced off the | Which options | Effect here |
|---|---|---|
| Left tail, low strikes | out-of-the-money puts and in-the-money calls | lighter tail, so cheaper |
| Right tail, high strikes | out-of-the-money calls and in-the-money puts | heavier tail, so more expensive |

So out-of-the-money puts get cheaper and in-the-money puts get more expensive. Equivalently, in-the-money calls get cheaper and out-of-the-money calls more expensive. Implied volatility is therefore an increasing function of strike, an upward-sloping or reverse skew.

a.reason: Out-of-the-money puts are struck low and become cheaper; in-the-money puts are struck high and become more expensive.

b.reason: Reversed for calls. Out-of-the-money calls are struck high and become more expensive here; in-the-money calls are struck low and become cheaper.

c.reason: At the money the call and the put share a strike and are locked together by put-call parity, so no change in the distribution can move the call down while moving the put up. This option describes an arbitrage rather than a plausible scenario, and can be eliminated on parity grounds alone.

d.reason: The exact reverse of the correct answer. It describes negative price-volatility correlation, that is, the standard equity case with a heavy left tail and a light right tail.

trap.explanation: Two mapping steps mean two chances to invert the direction. Anchor step two permanently: a high strike is priced off the right tail; an out-of-the-money put is struck low and an in-the-money put is struck high. Convert every moneyness label into a strike position before reasoning about tails. Option (c) is separately instructive because it can be killed by put-call parity alone, without any distributional reasoning.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A derivatives strategist is preparing an internal note on how the shape of the implied volatility curve reflects the implied distribution of log returns. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A platykurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis below 3, produces a symmetric smile.
A leptokurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis above 3, produces an inverted smile, or frown.
A normal mixture implied log return distribution produces a frown, because mixing two normal distributions reduces kurtosis below 3.
A platykurtic implied log return distribution produces a frown, in which at-the-money options carry a higher implied volatility than both deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the sign of excess kurtosis in the implied log return distribution determines whether the volatility curve smiles or frowns.

BSM assumes normally distributed log returns, kurtosis exactly 3. Deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options are priced off the tails; at-the-money options are priced off the centre.

| Implied log return distribution | Tails versus normal | Wing options | Curve shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| Leptokurtic, kurtosis above 3 | Heavy, worth more than BSM says | expensive | Smile |
| Platykurtic, kurtosis below 3 | Light, worth less than BSM says | cheap | Frown |
| Normal, kurtosis equal to 3 | as assumed, correctly priced | -- | Flat |

The mechanism is direct: heavier tails than BSM assumes mean the market pays more for wing options than a single constant volatility would justify, and because vega is positive, paying more means backing out a higher implied volatility. Both wings lift and the curve smiles.

The normal mixture case: a mixture of two normal distributions with different variances always has kurtosis above 3, even though each component is normal. Mixing variances fattens the tails, so a normal mixture produces a smile. This is also the link to conditional heteroskedasticity: a GARCH process is conditionally normal but unconditionally heavy tailed.

a.reason: Light tails give a frown, not a smile. The direction is reversed.

b.reason: Heavy tails give a smile, not a frown. The direction is reversed the other way.

c.reason: Two defects in one statement. A normal mixture has kurtosis above 3, not below, and it therefore produces a smile rather than a frown.

d.reason: Light tails depress both wings, leaving the at-the-money point highest, which is a frown.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (b) form a clean reversal of direction: if you cannot state which way excess kurtosis pushes the wings, both read as plausible. The memory hook is that fat tails make the wings expensive, and expensive wings lift the curve into a smile. Option (c) is the normal-mixture trap and is worth memorising separately, because "a mixture of normals must still be roughly normal" is a strong and wrong intuition.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing | Describe the equity and FX smiles and explain their shape
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: An options market maker is explaining to a graduate trainee that the implied volatility curve is computed from observed market prices and is therefore sensitive to order flow, not only to beliefs about the true distribution. Which of the following is most likely to steepen the downward-sloping skew typically observed in equity index options?

options.text: Event-driven hedge funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money call options on takeover candidates.
An increase in the risk-free rate used to discount all option payoffs.
Market makers becoming more willing to write high-delta call options and less willing to write low-delta call options.
End users such as pension funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money put options for downside protection.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: implied volatility is a function of the observed price, so supply and demand shift the curve independently of any change in beliefs about the distribution.

The equity skew is high implied volatility at low strikes and low implied volatility at high strikes. Steepening it means pushing the left side up, the right side down, or both.

Option (d): out-of-the-money puts sit at low strikes. Excess demand bids their prices up, and a higher price at a low strike backs out a higher implied volatility on the left, steepening the skew. This is the demand-side expression of crashophobia (Rubinstein).

Option (a): out-of-the-money calls sit at high strikes. Excess demand there lifts the right side, which flattens the skew and, if strong enough, reverses it.

Option (c): convert delta into strike before reasoning. A high-delta call is deep in the money and struck low; a low-delta call is out of the money and struck high. Greater willingness to write high-delta calls adds supply at low strikes, depressing left-side implied volatility, while reduced willingness to write low-delta calls lifts the right side. Both effects flatten the skew. The curriculum case runs the other way: writers who prefer low-delta calls increase the supply of out-of-the-money calls, depress their price and depress right-side implied volatility, which steepens the skew.

a.reason: Bids up the high-strike, right-hand side of the curve, which flattens rather than steepens the downward skew. The correct mechanism is applied to the wrong wing.

b.reason: The risk-free rate enters the BSM formula identically when implied volatility is extracted and when the option is priced, so it shifts price levels without a systematic strike-dependent effect on curve shape. It is outside the set of mechanisms that can change the slope.

c.reason: Assigns the wrong strike region to each delta. High-delta calls are struck low, so greater willingness to write them adds supply on the left and depresses left-side implied volatility. Combined with reduced supply on the right, the net effect flattens the skew.

d.reason: Bids up the low-strike, left-hand side, steepening the skew. This is crashophobia expressed as order flow.

trap.explanation: Option (c) survives a careless read because every intermediate step still sounds correct, but a high-delta call is struck low, and getting that mapping backwards inverts the entire conclusion. Option (b) is the irrelevant-parameter trap: it moves prices without moving shape.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing | Describe FX rate distributions and their implications
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: Most participants in a currency options market treat exchange rates as lognormally distributed and use a single constant volatility across all strikes in BSM. A risk analyst has concluded that the true distribution has materially heavier tails than lognormal on both sides, and she is indifferent to the direction of the move. Which trade most directly exploits her view?

options.text: Long butterfly
Short straddle
Long bull spread
Long strangle

questions.solution:
Concept tested: a smile-shaped mispricing is a long-volatility, direction-neutral view concentrated in the wings, which points to a strangle rather than a straddle.

If both tails are heavier than the market's flat-volatility model implies, then deep out-of-the-money options on both sides are systematically underpriced. She wants to be long precisely those instruments and neutral on direction.

A long strangle buys an out-of-the-money call at a high strike and an out-of-the-money put at a low strike. Both legs are the underpriced instruments and the combination has no directional bias.

A long straddle would also express a long-volatility, direction-neutral view, but it buys at-the-money options, and the at-the-money strike is exactly where the lognormal assumption is least wrong. The strangle concentrates the position where the mispricing lives.

Discipline: check the sign of net vega. Both legs of a strangle are long options, so net vega is positive, matching a long-volatility view.

a.reason: A long butterfly is long the two wing strikes and short two at-the-money options. Net vega is negative and it profits when the underlying pins near the middle strike, so it is a short-volatility trade. It is the near neighbour of the strangle because it also involves wing options, but the net exposure has the opposite sign.

b.reason: Sells volatility outright, the exact opposite of her view, and loses most severely in precisely the heavy tails she expects.

c.reason: A bull spread is a directional view on the underlying rising. The stem states explicitly that she is indifferent to direction, so this violates a stated condition of the question.

d.reason: Long out-of-the-money call plus long out-of-the-money put: long volatility, direction-neutral, concentrated in the wings.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the strongest distractor precisely because a butterfly does involve wing options, so it pattern-matches to "the tails are mispriced", but the distinction is between being net long the wings (strangle) and being long the wings only as protection while short the body (butterfly). Check the sign of net vega before choosing.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing | Describe FX rate distributions and their implications | Describe the equity and FX smiles and explain their shape | Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a smile
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question:
A volatility trader uses four labels for the archetypal shapes of the implied volatility curve plotted against $K/S$: SMILE (both wings elevated), FROWN (both wings depressed, at-the-money highest), DOWNWARD SKEW (implied volatility decreasing in strike) and UPWARD SKEW (implied volatility increasing in strike). Consider four scenarios.

I. The asset's volatility is positively correlated with the asset's price.
II. The underlying's price distribution has a heavy left tail and a thin right tail.
III. The underlying is an exchange rate that a central bank holds inside a very narrow band.
IV. The option matures in one week and, because of an imminent announcement, the underlying stock is expected to jump by more than 16% either up or down within the week.

Which sequence of shapes correctly corresponds to scenarios I through IV?

options.text: I. Upward skew, II. Downward skew, III. Frown, IV. Frown
I. Smile, II. Downward skew, III. Upward skew, IV. Smile
I. Downward skew, II. Upward skew, III. Frown, IV. Smile
I. Upward skew, II. Downward skew, III. Smile, IV. Smile

questions.solution:
Concept tested: mapping four distinct economic mechanisms onto four curve shapes. The single anticipated jump is the counterintuitive one and decides the question.

Scenario I. Positive price-volatility correlation stretches the upper tail and compresses the lower one: heavy right, light left. High strikes become expensive and low strikes cheap, so implied volatility increases in strike: upward skew.

Scenario II. Heavy left and thin right is the standard equity pattern by construction. Low strikes expensive, high strikes cheap, implied volatility decreases in strike: downward skew.

Scenario III. A currency pinned inside a narrow band cannot travel far in either direction. Both tails are truncated relative to lognormal, so both wings are cheap and the at-the-money point is relatively dearest: frown. This is the light-tailed platykurtic case.

Scenario IV. An anticipated large jump either up or down produces a bimodal distribution: mass piles up at two outcomes and the middle is hollowed out. The at-the-money option is struck in the hollow and is expensive relative to a lognormal benchmark with the same total variance, while the deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options sit beyond the two humps, where the distribution is actually thinner than lognormal, and are cheap. At-the-money implied volatility exceeds both wings: frown.

a.reason: Upward skew, downward skew, frown, frown.

b.reason: Assigns a smile to I, which requires both tails heavy whereas positive correlation lightens the left one. Assigns an upward skew to III, which requires a directional asymmetry a symmetric band does not create. Assigns a smile to IV, the classic jump error.

c.reason: Reverses I and II relative to the correct mapping, and again assigns a smile to IV.

d.reason: Gets I and II right, then fails on both III and IV. A narrow band thins the tails and a single jump hollows the middle. Neither elevates the wings, so neither produces a smile.

trap.explanation: Scenario IV decides this question and intuition points the wrong way: "jump" suggests "extreme move", which suggests "fat tails", which suggests "smile", but it is the reverse. Recurring random jumps of varying size give unconditional fat tails and a smile; one anticipated two-sided jump of known scale gives a bimodal distribution and a frown.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe FX rate distributions and their implications
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: An FX options desk observes that exchange rates satisfy neither of the two conditions required for an asset price to be lognormally distributed. Which statement about the resulting volatility smile is correct?

options.text: Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump; as option maturity increases, the volatility smile becomes less pronounced.
Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump; as option maturity increases, the volatility smile becomes more pronounced.
Exchange rates satisfy the constant volatility condition but violate the smooth-diffusion condition; the effect of jumps on implied volatility is independent of maturity.
Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump, but because both effects are strike-independent they shift the level of the curve without changing its shape.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the two conditions for lognormality, both of which FX violates, and the direction of the maturity effect on the pronouncedness of the smile.

Two conditions are required for an asset price to be lognormally distributed: (1) constant volatility of the asset, and (2) smooth price changes with no jumps, that is, a pure diffusion process.

Exchange rates violate both. FX volatility is stochastic and time varying, and FX rates jump on interventions, peg breaks and policy announcements. Hence the pronounced FX smile.

The maturity effect requires care, because the two channels behave differently and one behaves differently for prices than for implied volatilities:

| Channel | Effect on prices as maturity rises | Effect on implied volatility as maturity rises |
|---|---|---|
| Non-constant volatility | More pronounced | Less pronounced |
| Jumps | Less pronounced | Less pronounced |

The smile plots implied volatilities, so only the right-hand column governs its shape. Both channels weaken there, so the volatility smile becomes less pronounced as maturity increases. This is directly visible in any volatility surface: the one-month row is far more curved across strikes than the five-year row.

a.reason: Both conditions violated, and the smile flattens as maturity lengthens.

b.reason: Reverses the headline result. The smile becomes less, not more, pronounced with maturity.

c.reason: Two defects. FX volatility is not constant, so both conditions fail rather than one; and the impact of jumps is strongly maturity dependent, diminishing sharply as maturity lengthens. The option removes a condition that in fact fails and removes a dependence that in fact holds.

d.reason: If the two effects were strike-independent there would be no smile at all, only a parallel level shift. The claim asserts a completeness that contradicts the phenomenon under study.

trap.explanation: The split polarity is the trap: non-constant volatility has a more pronounced effect on prices and a less pronounced effect on implied volatilities as maturity rises. A candidate who has memorised only the phrase "more pronounced" will attach it to the wrong quantity. The discipline is to name the quantity before stating the direction.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe FX rate distributions and their implications
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A model validation analyst is reviewing the use of standard geometric Brownian motion, the pure diffusion process underlying BSM, across a set of currency exposures. For which of the following is standard GBM most likely to be an adequate representation of the price process?

options.text: A major, highly liquid currency pair.
A currency held at a fixed peg to another currency by its central bank.
An emerging market currency subject to periodic devaluations.
Any currency, provided the modelling horizon is short.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: which FX regimes are diffusion-like and which require an explicit jump component, and how the importance of jumps varies with the horizon.

Standard GBM is a pure diffusion: sample paths are continuous, so the process never moves by a discrete amount in an instant. It is adequate in markets deep and liquid enough that price discovery is close to continuous.

Major currency pairs trade in the deepest markets in the world with near-continuous order flow, so of the four this is where a diffusion fits best. Not perfectly, since even major pairs jump on central bank surprises, which is why the FX smile exists at all, but closest.

On the horizon question the relationship runs opposite to intuition: the shorter the horizon, the more important it is to model jumps. Over a short horizon there is little time for continuous diffusion to accumulate, so a single jump dominates the total variation. Over long horizons the contribution of jumps dissipates relative to accumulated diffusion and the process becomes hard to distinguish from a pure diffusion.

a.reason: Deep liquidity supports near-continuous price discovery, which is what a diffusion assumes.

b.reason: A peg is the archetypal jump process. The rate is pinned and does almost nothing, then moves discontinuously when the peg is realigned or breaks. A diffusion cannot generate that path.

c.reason: Emerging market currencies face devaluations, capital controls and regime shifts, all of which are discrete jumps rather than diffusion.

d.reason: Reverses the horizon relationship. At short horizons jumps matter most, because there is less diffusion to dilute them. It is at long horizons that the jump impact dissipates.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is attractive because "over a short period, less can happen" sounds correct, but it is exactly backwards for jump risk: over a short period the jump is essentially the only thing that can happen. This same asymmetry underlies the fact that the smile is most pronounced at short maturities.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the equity and FX smiles and explain their shape
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A CRO asks why equity index options display a pronounced downward-sloping volatility skew, rather than the roughly symmetric smile seen in currency options. Which pair of explanations is the one offered in the curriculum?

options.text: Capital structure leverage, whereby a fall in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money puts because they fear a repeat of a market crash.

Capital structure leverage, whereby a rise in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money calls because they fear missing a rally.
Mean reversion in equity volatility; and the fact that equity index options are cash-settled while currency options are physically settled.
The absence of natural two-sided hedging demand in equity markets; and the fact that equity prices are lognormally distributed while exchange rates are not.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the two curriculum explanations for the equity skew, one fundamental (financial leverage) and one behavioural or technical (crashophobia). Both push in the same direction.

Explanation 1: capital structure leverage. Firm value is split between debt and equity. If equity value falls while the debt load is roughly fixed, the debt-to-equity ratio rises. Higher financial leverage amplifies the effect of a given change in enterprise value on the residual equity claim, so equity volatility rises. Falling price implies rising volatility, a negative price-volatility relationship, which fattens the left tail and lifts implied volatility at low strikes.

The magnitude is material. In the curriculum illustration, a firm with EBIT of 20 million and EBIT volatility of 20% that takes on perpetual interest expense of 10 million per year sees equity volatility roughly double to about 37%, holding the price-to-earnings multiple constant. Raising interest expense to 15 million takes equity volatility to roughly 74%. With zero debt, equity volatility equals EBIT volatility exactly.

Explanation 2: crashophobia. Rubinstein's explanation, dated to the October 1987 crash. Participants attach more weight to a sharp downward move than a lognormal distribution permits, either because they believe the probability is genuinely higher or because out-of-the-money puts are demanded as catastrophe insurance. Either way those puts, which are struck low, are bid up, lifting implied volatility on the left.

Both explanations raise implied volatility at low strikes, so both produce the same downward-sloping skew.

a.reason: Both clauses state the correct direction and the correct instrument.

b.reason: Two reversals. Leverage rises when equity falls, not when it rises; and crashophobia concerns out-of-the-money puts bought as crash insurance, not calls bought for upside.

c.reason: Mean reversion in volatility explains the shape of the volatility term structure across maturities, not the smile across strikes. That is the neighbouring concept. The settlement mechanism has no bearing on the implied distribution at all.

d.reason: The second clause is self-defeating: if equity prices were genuinely lognormally distributed there would be no skew to explain, so the option assumes away its own subject. The first clause is not a curriculum explanation.

trap.explanation: Option (b) reverses the direction in both halves at once, and each half is individually plausible-sounding, so the discipline is to say the chain out loud and in order: equity price down, leverage up, volatility up, and crashophobia is about buying puts. Option (c) is the smile-versus-term-structure confusion that also appears elsewhere in this material.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe volatility term structures and surfaces and their use in pricing
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: The volatility term structure for options on an equity index is currently downward sloping, with short-dated implied volatilities well above long-dated implied volatilities. Which would be the most plausible explanation?

options.text: Mean reversion in volatility
Platykurtosis in returns, relative to lognormal
Serial correlation in returns
Independence of successive returns

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the volatility term structure as an expectation of average future volatility, and mean reversion as the mechanism capable of generating either slope.

The term structure plots implied volatility against time to maturity at a given strike. A long-dated implied volatility is, loosely, the market's expectation of average volatility over the life of the option.

Mean reversion means volatility is pulled back toward a long-run level: short-dated volatility high implies expected to fall implies downward-sloping term structure; short-dated volatility low implies expected to rise implies upward-sloping term structure.

Mean reversion is the only one of the four candidates that can produce either slope depending on the current level, which is exactly what makes it the explanation for a term structure shape. Given that short-dated volatility is currently high, it delivers the observed downward slope.

a.reason: With short-dated volatility currently high, mean reversion implies declining forecasts across horizons and therefore a downward slope.

b.reason: Confuses the two dimensions of the volatility surface. Platykurtosis, meaning light tails, is a statement about the return distribution at a given horizon, so it affects the smile across strikes and produces a frown. It says nothing about the slope across maturities.

c.reason: Positive serial correlation causes variance to scale faster than linearly in time, raising long-horizon annualised volatility relative to short-horizon. That implies an upward slope, the reverse of what is observed.

d.reason: Independence delivers the square-root-of-time rule, under which annualised volatility is identical at every horizon. That implies a flat term structure, which does not meet the condition stated in the stem.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the smile-versus-term-structure confusion and is the highest-frequency error here, because "platykurtosis" is a familiar smile-related word that pattern-matches to this reading. Always ask which axis the question concerns: variation across strikes is the smile, variation across maturities is the term structure.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe volatility term structures and surfaces and their use in pricing
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: An analyst states that if observed volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, then an upward-sloping volatility term structure is implied. Which is the most appropriate assessment of this statement?

options.text: Correct, because GARCH(1,1) assigns declining weights to older observations, which raises long-horizon volatility.
Correct, because GARCH(1,1) includes a long-run variance term, which is always above the current conditional variance.
Incorrect, because GARCH(1,1) implies mean reversion in volatility, so the term structure slopes upward or downward depending on whether current volatility is below or above the long-run level.
Incorrect, because GARCH(1,1) implies no relationship between current volatility and expected future volatility.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: GARCH(1,1) is a mean-reverting variance process, so it generates either slope. The direction is set by the current level relative to the long-run level, not by the model.

In GARCH(1,1) the conditional variance is a weighted average of three terms: a long-run variance, the previous period's squared return, and the previous conditional variance, with the three weights summing to one. The presence of a fixed long-run variance carrying positive weight is exactly what makes the process mean reverting: variance forecasts at increasing horizons converge geometrically toward the long-run level.

Current variance above long-run implies forecasts decline with horizon implies downward slope. Current variance below long-run implies forecasts rise with horizon implies upward slope.

The model alone does not determine the direction; the current level relative to the long-run level does. The analyst's statement is false as an unconditional claim.

a.reason: Declining weights on older observations describe the memory of the process, that is, the speed at which forecasts revert. Speed is not direction, so the stated reason does not support the stated conclusion.

b.reason: The long-run variance is a fixed parameter that can sit above or below the current conditional variance. The claim that it is "always above" asserts a universality that is simply false.

c.reason: Mean reversion generates either slope; the current level selects which.

d.reason: Reverses the defining property. GARCH(1,1) is characterised by a strong dependence of expected future variance on current variance; that dependence merely decays as the horizon lengthens, it does not vanish.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is a true statement about GARCH attached to a false conclusion, which makes it harder to reject than option (b)'s outright claim of universality. The general rule is that any answer committing a mean-reverting process to one particular slope, without conditioning on the current level, is wrong.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a smile
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A stock trades at USD 50.00. A regulatory decision will be announced within the next week, and the market is confident that the stock will jump sharply either up or down when it lands. A trader is pricing one-week options across a range of strikes. What shape should the implied volatility curve take, and why?

options.text: A pronounced smile, because the anticipated jump fattens both tails of the distribution relative to lognormal.
A downward-sloping skew, because the possibility of a sharp fall fattens the left tail.

A frown, because the anticipated jump makes the distribution bimodal, so at-the-money options are expensive relative to a lognormal benchmark while deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options are cheap.
A flat curve, because a jump affects the level of volatility but not its variation across strikes.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: a single anticipated two-sided jump produces a bimodal, not a fat-tailed, distribution, and therefore a frown rather than a smile.

The key is what the distribution actually looks like. The market is not saying that extreme moves are open-endedly more likely than lognormal allows. It is saying the stock will end up in one of two places and is unlikely to sit still. The terminal distribution is bimodal: two humps with a hollow in the middle where the current price sits.

Price options against a lognormal benchmark calibrated to the same total variance:

| Strike region | Probability mass versus lognormal | Option price | Implied volatility |
|---|---|---|---|
| At the money, in the hollow | Lower near the centre, higher at moderate distances either way | Expensive | High |
| Deep in and deep out, beyond the humps | Lower; the distribution does not extend far past the humps | Cheap | Low |

The curve is therefore highest at the money and falls away on both sides: a frown, the inverse of a smile.

a.reason: This is the trap the question is built around, and it reverses the effect. "Jump" and "fat tails" are not the same object. A single anticipated jump concentrates mass at two points; it empties the middle rather than extending the extremes.

b.reason: The stem is explicit that the jump can go either way, so there is no directional asymmetry to generate a skew. A downward skew requires the left tail to be heavier than the right, which the stated condition rules out.

c.reason: Bimodal distribution, hollow centre, expensive at-the-money options, cheap wings, hence a frown.

d.reason: A bimodal distribution differs from lognormal in shape, not merely in scale, so it necessarily affects strikes differentially. A pure level effect would leave the curve flat, which is ruled out by the scenario.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is a polarity trap worth committing to memory, because intuition points the wrong way. Rehearse it as a matched pair: recurring random jumps of varying size, as in currencies, generate unconditional fat tails and a smile; a single anticipated two-sided jump of known approximate scale generates a bimodal distribution and a frown. Same word, opposite curve.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: In January 2016 the Basel Committee issued its revised framework for market risk capital, known as the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book. Compared with Basel I and Basel II.5, each of the following is true about the FRTB EXCEPT which one, which is FALSE?

options.text: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the sum of two components, current VaR plus stressed VaR, whereas the FRTB requires only a single stressed expected shortfall.

The internal models approach under Basel I and II.5 calculated market risk capital using a single 10-day horizon, whereas the FRTB uses five different liquidity horizons depending on the liquidity of the market variable.
The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the default risk charge, which the FRTB eliminates, so that total market risk capital requirements are expected to fall.

The internal models approach under Basel I and II.5 calculated the requirement from VaR at a 99.0% confidence level, whereas the FRTB calculates it from expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the four headline changes from Basel I and Basel II.5 to the FRTB, and the direction of the resulting capital impact.

Lay the three regimes side by side under the internal models approach:

| Regime | Market risk capital under the IMA |
|---|---|
| Basel I | Current 99% 10-day VaR, obtained as $\sqrt{10}$ times the 99% one-day VaR |
| Basel II.5 | Two components: current 99% 10-day VaR plus stressed 99% 10-day VaR. Adds the incremental risk charge for credit-dependent instruments. |
| FRTB | One component: 97.5% stressed expected shortfall, with each variable's horizon set by its liquidity horizon. The IRC is replaced by the default risk charge. |

Statement (c) fails on two separate counts, either sufficient to make it the answer. First, the direction of the replacement is reversed: Basel II.5 had the incremental risk charge, and the FRTB does not eliminate a default charge, it replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which is introduced by the FRTB, not removed by it. Second, the capital impact runs the other way: on end-June 2015 data the revised framework was likely to produce an approximate median increase of 22% and a weighted average increase of 40% in total market risk capital requirements, with market risk RWAs rising from roughly 6% to just under 10% of total RWAs.

a.reason: True, and one of the defining simplifications of the FRTB. Basel II.5 summed a current-period and a stressed-period measure; the FRTB collapses this to a single stressed measure calibrated to a 12-month stressed period.

b.reason: True. The fixed 10-day horizon is replaced by five liquidity horizons assigned by risk factor.

c.reason: False, and therefore the answer. The IRC is replaced by the DRC rather than a default charge being eliminated, and capital rises rather than falls.

d.reason: True, and the single most-tested fact in the reading. The measure moves from 99% VaR to 97.5% expected shortfall.

trap.explanation: The EXCEPT format means the search is for the one false claim, and it buries its falsity in a plausible chain: the first half swaps the incremental risk charge for the default risk charge, two adjacent charges from consecutive regimes, and the second half reverses the direction of the capital impact. A candidate who knows only that "the FRTB changed the credit charge" will nod at the first half and never reach the second.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations | Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: One of the issues addressed extensively in the FRTB concerns the regulatory treatment of the trading book relative to the banking book. Which of the following is the major motivation behind these modifications?

options.text: Internal fraud in trading operations
Default risk on securitised exposures
Interest rate risk in the banking book
Regulatory arbitrage between the two books

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the economic problem the boundary rules solve, banks choosing the book that carries the lower capital charge for the same economic exposure.

Under the pre-FRTB framework the two books carried different treatments:

| | Trading book | Banking book |
|---|---|---|
| Intent | Intent to trade | Intent to hold to maturity |
| Valuation | Marked to market daily | Not marked to market daily |
| Capital | Market risk capital | Credit risk capital |

Because a credit-dependent instrument generally attracted a lower capital charge in the trading book, banks had an incentive to book it there even where the economic intent was closer to holding. Where the intent test was subjective and positions could be moved between books, the boundary became a lever for reducing required capital without reducing risk: regulatory arbitrage.

The FRTB responds twice: it makes the boundary more objective, with assignment fixed at initiation and strict limits on movement; and it introduces the default risk charge so that jump-to-default risk in the trading book is capitalised comparably with the banking book.

a.reason: Internal fraud is an operational risk concern, capitalised under a different framework entirely. It has no bearing on where an instrument is booked for market risk purposes.

b.reason: Default risk on securitised exposures is addressed by the FRTB, which requires securitisations to be capitalised under the standardised approach. That is a consequence of the framework rather than the reason for redrawing the boundary.

c.reason: Interest rate risk in the banking book is a real and separately regulated topic governed by its own standard. It is the neighbouring concept, not the motivation for the boundary changes.

d.reason: The boundary rules exist to close the capital gap that let banks choose their charge.

trap.explanation: Every distractor names a genuine risk the Basel framework addresses somewhere, which is what makes them plausible. The discipline is to ask what problem the boundary specifically solves: a boundary between two regimes is only a problem when the regimes differ in cost and the firm can choose its side, which is arbitrage by definition.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A risk analyst is presenting to a group of newly hired analysts on the change in risk measure introduced by the FRTB. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 99% confidence level, which is materially more conservative for every distribution.

The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level. For a normal distribution the two are almost exactly equivalent, but for a heavier-tailed distribution the 97.5% expected shortfall can be much greater than the 99% VaR.
The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, which is necessarily lower than 99% VaR because the confidence level has been reduced.
The FRTB retains 99% VaR but requires it to be calculated over a stressed period rather than a current period.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the confidence level of the new measure, and why the Committee could lower the confidence level without lowering the capital charge.

The FRTB moves the internal models measure from value at risk at 99% confidence to expected shortfall at 97.5% confidence. The confidence level appears to fall, but the measure changes from a quantile to a tail average, and the two effects roughly cancel under normality.

$$\text{99.0\% VaR} = \mu + 2.326\sigma \qquad \text{97.5\% ES} = \mu + 2.338\sigma$$

The multipliers differ by roughly half of one percent, so under normality the switch is close to capital neutral. That was deliberate: the Committee wanted a coherent, tail-sensitive measure without a mechanical recalibration of the level.

The change bites where intended. VaR is a quantile and is blind to the shape of the loss distribution beyond it, while expected shortfall averages the whole tail. For a distribution with a heavier tail than the normal, the 97.5% expected shortfall can be much greater than the 99% VaR. Expected shortfall is also coherent, satisfying subadditivity, which VaR does not.

a.reason: Substitutes 99% for the correct 97.5% confidence level, taking the parameter from the old measure. The word "every" also asserts a universality the reading does not support.

b.reason: Correct level, correct equivalence under normality, correct direction of the divergence for heavy tails.

c.reason: Reverses the effect of the calibration. Lowering the confidence level from 99% to 97.5% is offset by moving from a quantile to a tail average, which is why the multipliers come out at 2.326 and 2.338. "Necessarily lower" is false.

d.reason: The FRTB does not retain VaR as the capital measure. VaR survives only in the backtest, which is the adjacent role it is being confused with.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the intuitive trap: a lower confidence level sounds like a lower number. Holding the two multipliers, 2.326 and 2.338, in memory as a pair is the fastest way to reject it. Option (d) catches candidates who know VaR is still somewhere in the FRTB but cannot say where: VaR is in the backtest, not the capital charge.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: Under Basel II.5, banks were required to calculate a stressed VaR measure in addition to the current VaR measure. Over what length of stressed period is the stressed VaR calibrated?

options.text: A 10-day period
A 120-day period
A 250-day period
A 500-day period

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the calibration window for the stressed measure, which the FRTB inherits, and its separation from the several other numbers in this chapter that are 250 or nearby.

Basel II.5 required a stressed VaR alongside current VaR, calculated from the behaviour of market variables during a 250-day period of stressed market conditions, roughly one trading year. Banks searched back through history for the 250-day window that would have been most difficult for their current portfolio.

The FRTB carries this forward: capital is based on the expected shortfall of a 12-month stressed period, the same window expressed in months.

This chapter contains several numbers in the same neighbourhood that must be kept apart:

| Number | What it is |
|---|---|
| 250 days | Length of the stressed calibration period, Basel II.5 and FRTB |
| 250 trials | Number of overlapping 10-day historical simulation trials in the FRTB expected shortfall calculation |
| 120 days | Longest liquidity horizon in the final FRTB standard |
| 12 months | Backtesting data window, and the window used in the subset scaling ratio |

a.reason: 10 days is the Basel I and II.5 capital horizon for VaR and the base shock period in the FRTB expected shortfall calculation. Correct number, wrong role.

b.reason: 120 days is the longest liquidity horizon in the final FRTB. Different concept and different dimension of the framework.

c.reason: 250 days, equivalently 12 months, of stressed market conditions.

d.reason: 500 days is two trading years and is a common backtesting window in the exception-count literature. It is not the stressed calibration period.

trap.explanation: Every distractor is a real number from this material attached to the wrong concept, which is the entire design. The table of numbers is best learned as a unit rather than individually, because on the exam they will be offered in each other's slots.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: Under the FRTB standardised approach, the market risk capital requirement is the simple sum of three components. Which of the following is NOT one of those components?

options.text: A risk charge calculated under the sensitivities-based method
A residual risk add-on
A default risk charge
An incremental risk charge

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the three-part structure of the standardised approach, and the fact that the incremental risk charge belongs to the regime the FRTB replaced.

The standardised approach capital requirement is the simple sum of exactly three components:

| Component | What it captures |
|---|---|
| Sensitivities-based method charge | Delta, vega and curvature risk charges computed across seven risk classes |
| Default risk charge | Jump-to-default risk on credit-dependent and equity positions |
| Residual risk add-on | Risks the other two do not reach, in particular exotic underlyings and residual risks such as gap, correlation and behavioural risk |

The word simple is doing work: the three are added with no diversification benefit between them.

The incremental risk charge is not among them. It belongs to Basel II.5, where it capitalised default and migration risk for unsecuritised credit products in the trading book, and the FRTB replaces it with the default risk charge. It is the predecessor of a component, not a component.

a.reason: This is a component, and the largest of the three. It is where delta, vega and curvature charges are computed.

b.reason: This is a component, the catch-all for exotic underlyings and residual risks.

c.reason: This is a component, and it is the FRTB successor to the incremental risk charge.

d.reason: Not a component. The incremental risk charge is the Basel II.5 measure the FRTB's default risk charge replaces.

trap.explanation: Both terms, the incremental risk charge and the default risk charge, appear in the same option list, so a candidate who knows there is "a charge for default risk in the standardised approach" but has not fixed which acronym names it will find (c) and (d) equally plausible. Binding the timeline resolves it: the incremental risk charge is Basel II.5 and is gone; the default risk charge is FRTB and is one of the three.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: Under the sensitivities-based method within the FRTB standardised approach, a delta, vega and curvature risk charge is computed for each of seven risk classes. Which of the following is NOT one of those risk classes?

options.text: Credit spread risk, securitisation (correlation trading portfolio)
Funding liquidity risk
General interest rate risk
Commodity risk

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the seven sensitivities-based risk classes, and the distinction between a risk class and a risk charge type.

The sensitivities-based method defines seven risk classes:

| # | Risk class |
|---|---|
| 1 | General interest rate risk |
| 2 | Credit spread risk, non-securitisation |
| 3 | Credit spread risk, securitisation (non-CTP) |
| 4 | Credit spread risk, securitisation (CTP) |
| 5 | Equity risk |
| 6 | Commodity risk |
| 7 | Foreign exchange risk |

For each class three risk charges are computed and then aggregated: delta (first order) plus vega (sensitivity to volatility) plus curvature (second order).

Funding liquidity risk is not among the seven and is not a market risk class at all. It is the risk of being unable to meet obligations as they fall due, addressed by the liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio, which are ratios rather than capital charges. Market liquidity does enter the FRTB, but through the liquidity horizons inside the internal models calculation, not as a class.

Note the class versus charge distinction carefully: volatility is not a separate risk class; sensitivity to volatility is captured by the vega risk charge computed within each of the seven classes.

a.reason: This is a class, and the one most often doubted. Credit spread risk is split into three separate classes: non-securitisation, securitisation outside the correlation trading portfolio, and securitisation within it.

b.reason: Not a class. Funding liquidity risk is governed by the LCR and NSFR, which sit outside the market risk capital framework entirely.

c.reason: This is a class, and the first of the seven.

d.reason: This is a class, one of the seven.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is a trap in the opposite direction: a real class that sounds too specific to be one, so a candidate hunting the odd one out may pick it on grounds of unfamiliarity. Credit spread occupies three of the seven slots, the least intuitive feature of the list, and volatility is a charge applied within classes rather than a class of its own.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: In June 2017 the Basel Committee proposed a simplified version of the standardised approach for calculating market risk capital. Which of the following entities is it intended for?

options.text: Global systemically important banks with large and complex trading operations.
Banks whose trading desks have failed the backtesting exception thresholds.
Banks with material securitisation exposures.
Banks with a low concentration of trading book activity, or that lack the infrastructure to implement the sensitivities-based method.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: proportionality in the framework. The simplified standardised approach is a concession to small or unsophisticated banks, not a sanction imposed on failing ones.

The full standardised approach is itself demanding: the sensitivities-based method requires delta, vega and curvature sensitivities across seven risk classes with prescribed risk weights and correlations, which presupposes substantial infrastructure. For a small bank with a handful of trading positions the cost is disproportionate to the risk measured.

The simplified standardised approach therefore targets banks that either have a low concentration of trading book activity or lack the infrastructure to implement the sensitivities-based method successfully.

Keep the two directions of travel apart:

| Trigger | Destination |
|---|---|
| Small or unsophisticated bank, under supervisory permission | Simplified standardised approach |
| Desk fails backtesting or profit and loss attribution | Full standardised approach, imposed as a consequence |

a.reason: Global systemically important banks with large trading operations are precisely the institutions for which the simplified approach is inadequate. Their size and complexity demand the full standardised approach at minimum.

b.reason: The strongest distractor, and it points in the wrong direction. A desk that fails backtesting is moved to the full standardised approach as a sanction. Failure is not rewarded with a simplified calculation. The right destination is attached to the wrong trigger.

c.reason: Material securitisation exposures point towards more prescriptive treatment, not less. Securitisations must use the standardised approach in full and cannot use internal models at all.

d.reason: Low trading book concentration, or a lack of the infrastructure needed for the sensitivities-based method.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the intended kill because it correctly recalls that the standardised approach is where failing desks end up, then attaches that fact to the simplified variant. Separating a concession from a sanction resolves it: the simplified approach is granted to banks whose activity does not justify the full machinery, while the full standardised approach is imposed on desks whose models have failed.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations | Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
