questions.question: Both Basel 2.5 and the FRTB give firms two approaches for calculating market risk capital: a standardised approach and an internal models approach. Each of the following statements about the FRTB is true EXCEPT which one, which is FALSE?

options.text: Under the standardised approach, the capital requirement is the sum of three components: a sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge, and the residual risk add-on.
Under the internal models approach, the fixed 10-day liquidity horizon of Basel 2.5 is replaced by asset-class specific liquidity horizons of up to 120 days.
Under the internal models approach, the 99.0% VaR of Basel 2.5, both current and stressed, is replaced by a 97.5% stressed expected shortfall.

Under neither approach does the FRTB impose charges for credit-related exposures such as credit spread risk or jump-to-default risk, because those exposures are capitalised under the credit risk framework instead.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: whether trading book credit risk is capitalised inside the market risk framework, which is one of the defining features of the FRTB.

Statement (d) is false. The FRTB does not push trading book credit risk out to the credit risk framework. It capitalises it inside the market risk framework, explicitly and on both approaches:

| Approach | Credit spread risk | Jump-to-default risk |
|---|---|---|
| Standardised | Three of the seven sensitivities-based risk classes are credit spread classes: non-securitisation, securitisation outside the CTP, and securitisation within it | Capitalised through the default risk charge, one of the three components |
| Internal models | Handled like other market risks inside the expected shortfall, with liquidity horizons from 20 to 120 days | Capitalised on a one-year, 99.9% confidence VaR basis, mirroring the banking book |

Statement (d) also contradicts statement (a) within the same question, since (a) lists the default risk charge as a standardised approach component. In an EXCEPT question, if two options cannot both be true, one of them is the answer.

a.reason: True. The standardised approach requirement is the simple sum of the sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on.

b.reason: True. The single 10-day horizon is replaced by five liquidity horizons running from 10 up to 120 days under the final standard.

c.reason: True. This is the headline change in the risk measure.

d.reason: False. The FRTB explicitly capitalises both credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk within the market risk framework, on both approaches. The charge has been assigned to the wrong framework.

trap.explanation: Statement (d) is made plausible by a genuine fact: jump-to-default is capitalised using a banking-book style calibration of one year at 99.9%. A candidate who remembers that detail may conclude the exposure has been handed over to the credit risk framework, but borrowing a calibration is not the same as transferring the charge. The cross-option contradiction with (a) is the fastest route to the answer under time pressure.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare liquidity horizons and explain how a bank can calculate its ES
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A model risk analyst is documenting the liquidity horizons used under the internal models approach of the FINAL FRTB standard. Which of the following correctly states the five liquidity horizons and a correctly assigned example risk factor?

options.text: 10, 20, 60, 120 and 250 days; the credit spread on an investment grade corporate bond is assigned 60 days.
10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days; the credit spread on an investment grade corporate bond is assigned 40 days.
1, 10, 20, 60 and 250 days; the price of a large capitalisation equity is assigned 20 days.
10, 30, 60, 90 and 120 days; the price of a large capitalisation equity is assigned 30 days.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the five liquidity horizons in the final standard, and the assignment of common risk factors to them.

Basel I to III applied a single 10-day horizon to every risk factor, scaled from the one-day VaR by the square root rule: $\text{VaR}_{10\text{-day}} = \text{VaR}_{1\text{-day}} \times \sqrt{10}$.

The FRTB replaces that with five liquidity horizons, assigned by risk factor according to how long it would take to exit or hedge the position in a stressed market without materially moving prices. The final standard uses Category 1 = 10 days, Category 2 = 20 days, Category 3 = 40 days, Category 4 = 60 days, Category 5 = 120 days.

| Risk factor | Days | Risk factor | Days |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest rate, specified currencies | 10 | Equity price, large cap | 10 |
| Interest rate, other currencies | 20 | Equity price, small cap | 20 |
| Credit spread, sovereign IG | 20 | FX rate, specified pairs | 10 |
| Credit spread, corporate IG | 40 | FX rate, other pairs | 20 |
| Credit spread, corporate HY | 60 | Energy and carbon prices | 20 |
| Credit spread, volatility | 120 | Other commodities prices | 60 |

A structural check confirms the five values: the calculation shocks all variables over 10 days, then categories 2 to 5 over an additional 10 days, then categories 3 to 5 over an additional 20, then categories 4 and 5 over an additional 20, then category 5 over an additional 60. The cumulative horizons are 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120.

a.reason: These are the horizons proposed in the 2012 to 2014 consultative documents, which still appear in older textbook editions and question banks. The final standard replaced 60 with 40 and 250 with 120. Under the final rule an investment grade corporate credit spread carries 40 days, not 60.

b.reason: The five final horizons, with the investment grade corporate credit spread correctly placed in category 3 at 40 days.

c.reason: One day is not a liquidity horizon under any version of the FRTB; it is the backtesting horizon, a different dimension of the framework. A large capitalisation equity also carries the shortest horizon of 10 days, not 20; 20 days is the small cap assignment.

d.reason: Neither 30 nor 90 days appears anywhere in the schedule, and no version of the framework assigns 30 days to large capitalisation equity.

trap.explanation: This item exists because different sources disagree with each other, so an exam can too. Option (a) is not a fabrication; it is a previous, superseded answer from the consultative period. The anchor is the final five, 10 / 20 / 40 / 60 / 120, and the increment logic that generates them; a secondary trap sits inside the examples, since liquidity horizon rises with illiquidity, so large cap equity sits at the short end and credit spread volatility at the long end.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare liquidity horizons and explain how a bank can calculate its ES
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: Under the FRTB, the liquidity horizon plays a critical role in determining how much capital a bank must hold for a given risk factor. Which of the following best defines a liquidity horizon?

options.text: The time taken to find a willing buyer for a security or commodity.
The time taken to execute a sale that guarantees a minimum level of profit.
The time required to exit or hedge a risk position in a STRESSED market without materially affecting market prices.
The average time a position has been held on the trading desk's books.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the precise definition of the liquidity horizon, which contains three conditions that distractors are built by dropping.

The definition carries three elements and each is load bearing:

| Element | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Exit or hedge the position | A position can be neutralised without being sold. Definitions saying only "sell" are too narrow. |
| In a stressed market | Calibrated to conditions of stress, not to normal trading. This is what makes the horizons as long as they are. |
| Without materially affecting market prices | The constraint is price impact, not the mechanical availability of a counterparty. |

A longer liquidity horizon means a longer assumed unwind, a larger expected shortfall and a larger capital charge. The horizon is assigned by risk factor, not by instrument, and ranges from 10 to 120 days under the final standard.

a.reason: Drops the price impact condition and narrows the action to selling. Finding a willing buyer is necessary but not sufficient; the question is at what price impact the trade clears.

b.reason: Imports a profitability condition the definition does not contain. A profit test would make the horizon depend on entry price, which is irrelevant to liquidity.

c.reason: Captures all three elements: exit or hedge, stressed market, no material price impact.

d.reason: Holding period is a description of past behaviour and is the neighbouring concept. The liquidity horizon is a forward-looking regulatory assumption fixed by risk factor category regardless of how long the desk has actually held the position.

trap.explanation: Each wrong option is built by deleting or substituting exactly one condition and then reading plausibly without it. Reciting the definition as a three-part checklist and testing each option against all three parts, rather than accepting an option because nothing in it sounds actively wrong, is the safeguard.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare liquidity horizons and explain how a bank can calculate its ES
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: The FRTB requires a bank to calculate five partial expected shortfalls, $ES_1$ through $ES_5$, in order to reflect different liquidity horizons across risk factor categories. Which of the following best describes the method?

options.text: $ES_3$ is a 10-day shock applied to all variables in categories 3, 4 and 5 while categories 1 and 2 are held constant, then scaled by $\sqrt{40/10}$ to reach a 40-day equivalent. Total expected shortfall is the square root of the sum of the squares of the five scaled measures. The historical simulation uses 250 overlapping 10-day trials.

$ES_3$ is a 10-day shock applied to all variables in categories 3, 4 and 5 while categories 1 and 2 are held constant, then scaled by $\sqrt{40/10}$. Total expected shortfall is the simple sum of the five scaled measures, because variable changes are assumed perfectly correlated. The simulation uses 250 overlapping trials.

$ES_3$ is a 40-day shock applied directly to category 3 only, each category being shocked over its own horizon so no scaling is required. Total expected shortfall is the square root of the sum of the five unsquared partial measures.

$ES_3$ is a 40-day shock applied directly to category 3 only, and total expected shortfall is the simple sum of the five partial measures, because perfect correlation is the most conservative assumption. The simulation uses 250 non-overlapping trials.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the mechanics of the FRTB expected shortfall, nested shocks over a common 10-day base, square-root-of-time scaling to each liquidity horizon, and aggregation under an independence assumption.

The calculation has four features. The shocks are nested, not isolated: $ES_j$ shocks all variables in categories $j$ through 5 while holding categories $1$ through $j-1$ constant, each computed over a common 10-day base shock. Scaling is by the square root of time, from the 10-day base to the incremental horizon of the category:

$$ES = \sqrt{ES_1^2 + \sum_{j=2}^{5}\left[ES_j \times \sqrt{\frac{LH_j - LH_{j-1}}{LH_1}}\right]^2}$$

where $LH_j$ is the liquidity horizon of category $j$ and $LH_1 = 10$ days. Aggregation is root-sum-of-squares, not a simple sum, following directly from the framework's assumption that the successive incremental changes are independent; a simple sum would embed perfect correlation, which is more conservative but is not what the standard specifies. The trials overlap: trial 1 runs day 0 to day 10, trial 2 runs day 1 to day 11, and so on to trial 250 running day 249 to day 259, because a 250-day stressed period yields only 25 non-overlapping 10-day windows, far too few. Overlap costs effective sample size and makes the estimate noisier, though it does not bias it.

a.reason: Nested 10-day shocks, square-root scaling, root-sum-of-squares aggregation, 250 overlapping trials.

b.reason: Correct on the shock structure and the scaling, wrong on aggregation. A simple sum embeds perfect correlation, whereas the framework assumes independence and therefore the square root of the sum of squares. Being more conservative is not the same as being what the rule requires.

c.reason: Wrong on two counts. The shocks are nested over a common 10-day base and then scaled, rather than each category being shocked directly over its own horizon with the scaling step dropped. And a square root of a sum of unsquared measures is not a recognised, dimensionally coherent aggregation.

d.reason: Wrong on the shock structure, wrong on aggregation, and wrong on the trials. Non-overlapping 10-day trials over a 250-day window would yield only 25 observations, which is exactly why the framework specifies overlapping windows.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (b) are identical up to a single clause, root-sum-of-squares versus simple sum, and (b) is armed with the appealing phrase "most conservative assumption". Conservatism is not the test; the specified assumption is. Whenever a distractor justifies itself by being more prudent, it is worth checking whether prudence is actually the rule.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare liquidity horizons and explain how a bank can calculate its ES
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question:
A bank has calculated the five partial expected shortfalls below, each measured over a 10-day base shock, in EUR millions. The five liquidity horizons are 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days. Which is nearest to the total expected shortfall?

| Partial measure | $ES_1$ | $ES_2$ | $ES_3$ | $ES_4$ | $ES_5$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10-day base value (EUR m) | 40 | 30 | 20 | 12 | 6 |

options.text: EUR 55.50 million
EUR 61.68 million
EUR 73.70 million
EUR 108.00 million

questions.solution:
Concept tested: numerical application of the FRTB expected shortfall aggregation formula, including the incremental horizon scaling factors.

Step 1. Write the formula: $ES = \sqrt{ES_1^2 + \sum_{j=2}^{5}\left[ES_j \times \sqrt{(LH_j - LH_{j-1})/10}\right]^2}$.

Step 2. Compute the scaling factor for each category from the increment in its liquidity horizon, not from the horizon itself:

| Category | LH (days) | Increment | Scaling factor | Scaled value (EUR m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | base | 1.0000 | $40\times1.0000=40.000$ |
| 2 | 20 | $20-10=10$ | $\sqrt{10/10}=1.0000$ | $30\times1.0000=30.000$ |
| 3 | 40 | $40-20=20$ | $\sqrt{20/10}=1.4142$ | $20\times1.4142=28.284$ |
| 4 | 60 | $60-40=20$ | $\sqrt{20/10}=1.4142$ | $12\times1.4142=16.971$ |
| 5 | 120 | $120-60=60$ | $\sqrt{60/10}=2.4495$ | $6\times2.4495=14.697$ |

Step 3. Aggregate as the square root of the sum of squares:

$$40.000^2+30.000^2+28.284^2+16.971^2+14.697^2 = 1600+900+800+288+216=3804$$
$$ES=\sqrt{3804}\approx 61.68$$

The total expected shortfall is approximately EUR 61.68 million, which exceeds $ES_1$ alone of EUR 40 million because the longer horizons on the less liquid categories add materially. That is precisely the effect the liquidity horizon regime was designed to produce.

a.reason: EUR 55.50 million $=\sqrt{40^2+30^2+20^2+12^2+6^2}=\sqrt{3080}$. This aggregates correctly but omits the liquidity horizon scaling entirely, treating every category as if it had a 10-day horizon.

b.reason: EUR 61.68 million, computed above.

c.reason: EUR 73.70 million uses the consultative horizons of 10, 20, 60, 120 and 250 days, whose increments are 10, 40, 60 and 130 and whose factors are 1.0000, 2.0000, 2.4495 and 3.6056. The method is right and the horizon parameters are the stale, superseded ones.

d.reason: EUR 108.00 million $=40+30+20+12+6$, the simple sum of the unscaled partial measures. It makes two errors at once: no horizon scaling, and perfect-correlation aggregation instead of independence.

trap.explanation: Two distinct slips are policed. Option (a) is the scaling omission and option (c) is the stale-horizon error, the one most likely to appear on a source that has not been updated to the final standard. The subtler trap inside the correct path is scaling by the horizon rather than by the increment, for example using $\sqrt{40/10}$ for category 3 as a level rather than $\sqrt{20/10}$ as an increment, which inflates the answer.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare liquidity horizons and explain how a bank can calculate its ES
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A bank finds it difficult to identify past stressed periods using the full set of market variables, because historical data are unavailable for some of them. Which of the following correctly describes how the FRTB addresses this?

options.text: The bank may exclude the risk factors with insufficient historical data from its capital requirement calculation, so as not to overstate capital needs during stressed periods.

The bank may base the stressed period calculation on a SUBSET of market variables and scale the result up by the ratio of the expected shortfall for the most recent 12 months using ALL variables to the expected shortfall for the most recent 12 months using the SUBSET, provided the subset accounts for at least 75% of the expected shortfall.
The bank may substitute the standardised approach for the affected risk factors only, retaining the internal models approach for the remainder of the desk.
The bank may use a proxy stressed period drawn from a peer institution's data, subject to supervisory approval.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the FRTB accommodation for missing historical data, a subset calculation scaled by a ratio of expected shortfalls, with a coverage floor on the subset.

The stressed expected shortfall must be calibrated to a 12-month stressed period identified by searching history, and that search requires historical data for every variable. For some variables the data do not exist far enough back. The FRTB solution has three components, and a complete answer must contain all three:

$$ES_{\text{stressed, full}} = ES_{\text{stressed, subset}} \times \frac{ES_{\text{recent 12m, all variables}}}{ES_{\text{recent 12m, subset}}}$$

1. The subset: the stressed period calculation may be run on a reduced set of variables for which long histories exist.
2. The scaling ratio: the result is scaled up by the ratio of two expected shortfalls measured over the same recent 12-month window, one using all variables and one using the subset. Because both legs cover the same window, the ratio isolates the contribution of the omitted variables and is at least 1, so the adjustment is always upward.
3. The 75% floor: the subset must account for at least 75% of the expected shortfall of the full set, so that a bank cannot pick a trivially small subset and let the ratio do all the work.

a.reason: The FRTB does not permit risk factors to be dropped. Excluding a risk factor removes real risk from the capital calculation, which is the opposite of the framework's purpose, and the stated rationale inverts the regulatory objective.

b.reason: Subset, 12-month ratio scaling, 75% floor, all three present.

c.reason: A partial fallback to the standardised approach is not the remedy for data scarcity. The standardised approach is imposed at desk level and as a consequence of backtesting or profit and loss attribution failure, not as a data fix. The remedy has been assigned to the wrong trigger.

d.reason: The framework provides a scaling mechanism using the bank's own data over a common window. There is no peer-data substitution provision, so this invents a condition that does not exist.

trap.explanation: The 75% floor is the detail most often dropped, and a distractor can get the subset and the ratio right while omitting the floor. The second detail to fix is that both legs of the ratio use the most recent 12 months, not the stressed period; a distractor scaling by a stressed-period ratio would be self-defeating, since the stressed-period figure is the very quantity being estimated.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare liquidity horizons and explain how a bank can calculate its ES | Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: Each of the following is true about the internal models approach under the FRTB EXCEPT which one, which is FALSE?

options.text: The stressed period calculation may be based on a subset of market variables, scaled up provided the subset accounts for at least 75% of the expected shortfall.
The backtest must be conducted on the 97.5% stressed expected shortfall measure, so that the backtest uses the same measure as the capital charge.

The use of overlapping time periods is less than ideal because changes in successive historical simulation trials are not independent, but this does not bias the results; it reduces the effective sample size and makes the results noisier.

The capital charge is based on a weighted average of the expected shortfall for the whole portfolio and the sum of the partial expected shortfalls, where the partials are obtained by shocking the variables in one risk category while holding all others fixed.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: four separate features of the internal models approach, one contradicted by the reason the FRTB retained VaR in the backtest at all.

Statement (b) is false, for the reason that governs the whole backtesting design. It is not possible to backtest a stressed measure, because a stressed measure is calibrated to a historical period that is deliberately not the current period, so there is no set of realised outcomes to compare it against. Backtesting a 10-day expected shortfall is separately difficult, because expected shortfall is a tail average rather than a threshold and does not produce a clean count of exceptions. For both reasons the FRTB retains a value at risk backtest even though VaR is no longer the capital measure: a one-day static VaR, calibrated to the most recent 12 months equally weighted, reported at both the 97.5th and the 99th percentiles, at desk level.

On (d), the detail versus total issue: summing the expected shortfalls of the individual risk categories always produces a larger figure than the expected shortfall of the whole portfolio, because summing discards diversification across categories. Rather than choose one, the Committee specified a weighted average of the two, allowing partial but not full recognition of cross-category diversification.

a.reason: True. This is the data-scarcity accommodation, including the 75% coverage floor.

b.reason: False, and therefore the answer. A stressed measure cannot be backtested and expected shortfall is difficult to backtest, so the FRTB backtests VaR instead. The capital measure has been substituted for its neighbour, the backtest measure.

c.reason: True, and the precise wording matters. Overlapping windows induce dependence between successive trials, which costs effective sample size and therefore precision, but does not introduce bias.

d.reason: True. Because the sum of the partials exceeds the whole-portfolio figure, the Committee settled on a weighted average of the two.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is attractive because internal consistency sounds like good regulatory design: if capital is stressed expected shortfall, surely the backtest should test stressed expected shortfall. The FRTB deliberately accepts the inconsistency because the alternative is impossible. Option (c) hinges on the distinction between bias and noise, a pair of words a distractor could just as easily swap.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: A regulatory reporting analyst is preparing a summary of the differences between the trading book and the banking book. Which of the following correctly pairs the valuation treatment with the capital treatment?

options.text: Trading book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to market risk capital; banking book instruments are not marked to market daily and are subject to credit risk capital.
Trading book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to credit risk capital; banking book instruments are not marked to market daily and are subject to market risk capital.
Instruments in both books are marked to market daily under the FRTB, but only trading book instruments attract market risk capital.
Trading book instruments are valued at historical cost and are subject to market risk capital; banking book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to liquidity risk capital.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the two consequences that follow from the book assignment, and which capital regime attaches to which side of the boundary.

Assignment follows from intent, and two consequences follow from the assignment:

| | Trading book | Banking book |
|---|---|---|
| Intent | Intent to trade | Expected to be held to maturity |
| Valuation | Marked to market daily | Not marked to market daily; carried at amortised or historical cost |
| Capital regime | Market risk capital | Credit risk capital |
| Typical contents | Listed equities, exchange-traded derivatives, correlation trading portfolio, market-making inventory | Loans to customers, real estate holdings, unlisted equities, hedge fund holdings |

This pairing generates the arbitrage incentive: for a credit-dependent instrument the market risk charge was typically lighter than the credit risk charge, so booking it on the trading side reduced capital without reducing risk.

Liquidity risk does not have its own capital charge in this framework. Liquidity enters the FRTB through the liquidity horizons inside the market risk calculation, and is separately addressed by the LCR and NSFR, which are ratios rather than capital charges.

a.reason: Both pairings correct: mark to market with market risk capital on the trading side, no daily revaluation with credit risk capital on the banking side.

b.reason: The valuation treatments are right but the two capital regimes have been assigned to the wrong books. This is why it survives a casual read: the half most candidates remember is stated correctly.

c.reason: The FRTB did not extend daily mark to market to the banking book. Not marking the banking book to market is precisely why the boundary matters; if both books were revalued daily the accounting distinction would largely collapse.

d.reason: Both pairings are inverted, and it invents a liquidity risk capital charge that does not exist in this framework.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the intended kill because it gets the easy half right and buries the swap in the second clause, so checking both columns of a two-part statement independently is essential. Any answer choice inventing a "liquidity risk capital" charge can be eliminated on sight.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: Prior to the FRTB, the boundary between the regulatory banking book and the trading book created an opportunity for regulatory arbitrage. Which of the following is true about the treatment of that boundary under the FRTB?

options.text: The FRTB collapses the banking book and the trading book into a single book, which removes the arbitrage opportunity entirely.
The FRTB makes no change to the boundary but subjects both books to identical capital calculations.

The FRTB retains a subjective intent-to-trade test as the necessary and sufficient condition for trading book inclusion, and imposes the incremental risk charge as a penalty when a position is moved between books.
The FRTB establishes a more objective boundary, including assignment at the point a position is initiated and strict limits on subsequent movement between the books.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: how the FRTB closes the arbitrage, not by removing the boundary but by making it objective and making it sticky.

The pre-FRTB boundary failed for two related reasons: the test was largely subjective, resting on a stated intent to trade; and positions could be moved between books after initiation, so a bank could re-designate an instrument when relative capital cost shifted.

| Failure | FRTB response |
|---|---|
| The test was subjective | A more objective boundary, with presumptive lists of instruments assigned to each book and evidence-based criteria rather than stated intent alone |
| Positions could be re-designated | Assignment is made when the position is initiated, with strict limits on subsequent movement; a switch requires supervisory approval and any capital benefit from the switch is disallowed |

The FRTB does not merge the books. The distinction between held-to-maturity banking exposures and traded positions is economically real and the two continue to attract different capital regimes. The reform makes the line harder to game, not absent.

a.reason: The two books remain distinct under the FRTB and continue to attract credit risk capital and market risk capital respectively. Collapsing them would abolish a real economic distinction and overreaches what the reform did.

b.reason: Reverses the reform on both clauses. The FRTB does change the boundary, substantially, and the two books are not subjected to identical calculations; if they were there would be no boundary to police.

c.reason: Moves in the wrong direction on the intent test, and misidentifies the charge. The incremental risk charge is a Basel II.5 capital charge for credit-dependent trading book instruments, replaced by the default risk charge under the FRTB. It was never a penalty for reclassification.

d.reason: Objective criteria, assignment at initiation, strict limits on movement.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (b) are the two extreme readings, abolish the boundary or leave it alone, and both can be rejected by asking whether the described change would leave a distinction worth policing. Option (c) is the dangerous one, because it correctly names a real charge and attaches it to a function it never had.

questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question:
In order to determine which exposures attract credit risk capital and which attract market risk capital, a bank has classified eight instruments into the trading book or the banking book as shown below. How many of these classifications are correct?

| Assigned to the TRADING book | Assigned to the BANKING book |
|---|---|
| Listed equities | Unlisted equities |
| Hedge fund investments | Real estate holdings |
| Crude oil options with 30-day maturity | Mortgage loans extended to bank customers |
| Instruments in a correlation trading portfolio | Instruments resulting from market-making activities |

options.text: All eight are correctly classified.
Six are correctly classified and two are probably wrong.
Three are correctly classified and five are probably wrong.
All eight are wrongly classified.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: applying the boundary criteria to specific instruments, including the two presumptive assignments that most often catch candidates.

Work through the list against the intent test: trading book means intent to trade and daily revaluation; banking book means expected to be held to maturity.

| Instrument | Assigned | Correct book | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Listed equities | Trading | Trading | Correct |
| Hedge fund investments | Trading | Banking | Wrong |
| Crude oil options, 30-day | Trading | Trading | Correct |
| Correlation trading portfolio | Trading | Trading | Correct |
| Unlisted equities | Banking | Banking | Correct |
| Real estate holdings | Banking | Banking | Correct |
| Mortgage loans to customers | Banking | Banking | Correct |
| Market-making instruments | Banking | Trading | Wrong |

Six correct, two wrong. Hedge fund investments belong in the banking book: a hedge fund holding cannot be reliably marked to market daily and cannot be exited on demand, since redemption typically requires notice and may be gated, so it fails the daily revaluation and ready exit conditions. Instruments resulting from market-making activities belong in the trading book: market making is the paradigm case of intent to trade, and inventory held to service two-way client flow is not held to maturity by any reading.

a.reason: Would require hedge fund holdings in the trading book and market-making inventory in the banking book. Both are presumptively assigned the other way, so the condition for "all eight" is not met.

b.reason: Six correct, with hedge funds and market-making instruments both misplaced.

c.reason: Understates the bank's accuracy considerably. Six of the eight follow directly from the intent and revaluation criteria.

d.reason: The straightforward cases, listed equities, crude oil options, real estate and mortgage loans, are all placed correctly.

trap.explanation: The two errors are placed at opposite corners of the table so that a candidate who spots one and stops will answer "seven correct", which is not offered, and will then guess. Hedge funds read as trading because they are investments in traded strategies, but the test is whether the bank's own position can be marked and exited daily, not what the fund itself does. Market-making inventory reads as banking to anyone associating the banking book with "things the bank originates".

questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: In comparison with Basel III, which essentially carried forward the earlier quantitative backtesting requirements under the internal models approach, which of the following best summarises the change to the backtesting requirements under the FRTB?

options.text: The backtesting methodology is unchanged under the FRTB.
A one-day static VaR, calibrated to the most recent 12 months of data, is backtested at BOTH the 97.5th and the 99th percentiles, at the level of each individual trading desk.
There are two tests: a 10-day 99.0% expected shortfall and a 10-day 99.0% stressed VaR.
The 10-day horizon and the 99.0% confidence level are unchanged, but they are now applied to expected shortfall rather than to VaR.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the four attributes of the FRTB backtest that jointly distinguish it from the earlier regime: measure, horizon, confidence levels, and level of application.

| Attribute | FRTB requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Measure | Value at risk, not expected shortfall | Expected shortfall is hard to backtest and a stressed measure cannot be backtested at all |
| Horizon | One day | A one-day horizon yields roughly 250 usable observations per year; a 10-day horizon would not |
| Confidence levels | Both 97.5% and 99.0% | Two levels give two views of model accuracy, with separate exception thresholds |
| Level of application | Each individual trading desk | Failure consequences bite at desk level, not bank level |

The VaR is also static, calibrated to the most recent 12 months equally weighted, and compared against at least one year of the desk's current one-day profit and loss. This is why VaR survives the FRTB at all: it is no longer the capital measure but remains the validation measure, and the results feed the multiplicative parameters used to convert expected shortfall into the capital requirement.

a.reason: The methodology changes in every one of the four attributes above. Under Basel II.5 the backtest was of a single 99% one-day VaR; the FRTB adds the 97.5% level and pushes the test down to desk level with hard consequences.

b.reason: Correct measure, horizon, both confidence levels, and desk-level application.

c.reason: Substitutes the capital measure for the backtest measure. Neither expected shortfall nor a stressed measure is backtested under the FRTB.

d.reason: Also assembled entirely from the capital calculation. The backtest horizon is one day, not 10, and the measure is VaR, not expected shortfall.

trap.explanation: Options (c) and (d) both import the capital measure into the backtest, which is the single most common error in this material. Keeping the two columns apart in memory helps: capital is 97.5% stressed expected shortfall over liquidity horizons; backtesting is one-day VaR at 97.5% and 99% over the recent 12 months. The framework is deliberately inconsistent between them.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: The FRTB requires backtesting to be conducted using a VaR measure calculated over a one-day horizon and the most recent 12 months of data, rather than using the expected shortfall measure on which capital is based. What is the primary reason for this?

options.text: Expected shortfall is not a coherent risk measure and so cannot be validated statistically.
Backtesting a 10-day expected shortfall is difficult, and backtesting a STRESSED measure is in theory impossible, so a measure calibrated to current data is required.
One-day VaR backtesting improves the bank's ability to forecast long-term capital adequacy and aligns with stress testing across all risk types.
Regulators require the backtest measure to match the measure used for the standardised approach, which is based on VaR.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: why the FRTB accepts an inconsistency between its capital measure and its validation measure.

Two independent obstacles rule out backtesting the capital measure directly. Obstacle 1: expected shortfall is hard to backtest. A backtest compares predictions against realised outcomes; VaR produces a clean binary prediction that the loss will not exceed a threshold, giving a countable number of exceptions with a known binomial distribution, whereas expected shortfall is a tail average with no threshold to breach and therefore no natural count. Obstacle 2, the stronger objection: a stressed measure cannot be backtested at all, because it is calibrated to a historical stressed window rather than to current conditions, so comparing it against current realised profit and loss compares two different states of the world.

The FRTB therefore backtests a measure it does not use for capital. Regulators may additionally request other diagnostics, such as the p-value of the profit or loss on a given day, meaning the probability of experiencing a profit smaller than the actual profit; in theory those p-values should be uniformly distributed, and departures from uniformity signal model error.

a.reason: Reverses a well-known property. Expected shortfall is coherent, which is one of the principal reasons the FRTB adopted it over VaR. Coherence is in any case unrelated to backtestability.

b.reason: Both obstacles stated, with the stressed-measure objection correctly identified as the decisive one.

c.reason: Backtesting validates short-horizon model accuracy against realised outcomes. It does not forecast long-term capital adequacy, and it does not align with enterprise stress testing, which uses different horizons and scenario assumptions.

d.reason: The standardised approach is not based on VaR at all; it is the sum of a sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on. Backtesting applies to internal models, which is the only place a model exists to be validated.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the sharpest distractor because it deploys a true-sounding technical word in a reversed claim: coherence is exactly what expected shortfall has and VaR lacks. Option (d) ties backtesting to the standardised approach, which contains no model and therefore nothing to backtest, so it is disqualifying on its own.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: A risk manager compares a trading desk's one-day static VaR, calibrated to the most recent 12 months of data and equally weighted, at both the 97.5th and the 99th percentiles, against the desk's observed one-day profit and loss. Over the most recent 12-month period the desk experienced 13 exceptions at the 99th percentile and 32 exceptions at the 97.5th percentile. What is the required treatment?

options.text: The desk may continue to use the internal models approach, because 13 exceptions is within the tolerance of 30 that applies to backtesting exceptions.
The desk may continue to use the internal models approach for the 97.5% measure only, and must apply the standardised approach to the 99% measure.
All positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach, until the desk no longer exceeds the thresholds over the prior 12 months.
All positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach permanently, because internal models approval once withdrawn cannot be regained.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the desk-level backtesting exception thresholds, and the fact that the consequence is both all-or-nothing at desk level and reversible.

The rule: if a desk experiences either more than 12 exceptions at the 99th percentile or more than 30 exceptions at the 97.5th percentile in the most recent 12-month period, all of its positions must be capitalised using the standardised approach.

| Percentile | Threshold | Observed | Breached? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 99.0% | more than 12 | 13 | Yes |
| 97.5% | more than 30 | 32 | Yes |

Either breach alone would suffice; both are breached here. Three features of the consequence matter: it is desk level, applying to each desk individually; it is all or nothing for that desk, with no partial or measure-by-measure fallback; and it is reversible, with positions continuing under the standardised method until the desk no longer exceeds the thresholds over the prior 12 months.

For calibration, note the slack: over roughly 250 trading days one would statistically expect $1\% \times 250 = 2.5$ exceptions at the 99th percentile and $2.5\% \times 250 = 6.25$ at the 97.5th. Thresholds of 12 and 30 sit far above those expectations, deliberately, so that ordinary sampling variation does not disqualify a sound model.

a.reason: Swaps the two thresholds. The tolerance of 30 belongs to the 97.5th percentile; the 99th percentile tolerance is 12. Against the correct threshold, 13 exceptions is a breach.

b.reason: There is no measure-by-measure fallback. The consequence applies to all positions on the desk, and the 97.5% count of 32 is in any case also a breach.

c.reason: All positions on the desk move to the standardised approach, and the exclusion lifts once the desk is back inside both thresholds over the prior 12 months.

d.reason: The rule explicitly contemplates a return to the internal models approach once the thresholds are respected over the prior 12 months. Nothing about the withdrawal is permanent.

trap.explanation: The threshold swap in option (a) is the numerical trap and is easy to fall into because 13 and 30 are both plausible-looking pairings; binding each number to its percentile helps, since the tighter percentile carries the smaller allowance, so 99% goes with 12 and 97.5% goes with 30. Option (d) can be eliminated on the word "permanently" alone, since the rule contains an explicit reversal condition.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: A trading desk is undergoing profit and loss attribution testing. Let $U$ be the difference between the model's profit or loss on a given day and the actual, hypothetical profit or loss on that day, and let $V$ be the actual profit or loss. Which of the following observed values would constitute a FAILURE of the test?

options.text: $\text{Mean}(U)/\text{SD}(V) = 5\%$
$\text{Var}(U)/\text{Var}(V) = 18\%$
$\text{Mean}(U)/\text{SD}(V) = -8\%$
$\text{Var}(U)/\text{Var}(V) = 22\%$

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the two profit and loss attribution metrics and their thresholds, including the fact that one is two-sided and the other one-sided.

Profit and loss attribution tests whether the risk model actually explains the desk's realised outcomes, rather than merely producing an acceptable number of exceptions. It compares the model's profit and loss against the hypothetical profit and loss, that is, the profit or loss that would have occurred had there been no trading during the day, so that intraday trading does not contaminate the test.

| Metric | Formula | What it detects | Threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean ratio | $\text{Mean}(U)/\text{SD}(V)$ | Systematic bias in the model | must lie within $\pm10\%$ |
| Variance ratio | $\text{Var}(U)/\text{Var}(V)$ | Proportion of variation the model fails to explain | must not exceed 20% |

The mean ratio is two-sided, because bias in either direction is a defect: a model systematically overstating profit is as wrong as one understating it. The variance ratio is one-sided, because unexplained variance is only a problem when it is large.

Applying the thresholds: 5% is inside $\pm10\%$ and passes; 18% is below 20% and passes; $-8\%$ is inside $\pm10\%$ and passes; 22% exceeds 20% and fails.

a.reason: 5% lies comfortably inside the $\pm10\%$ band, so the failure condition is not met.

b.reason: 18% is below the 20% ceiling and passes, though close enough to warrant attention. It would fail only against the 10% threshold, which belongs to the other metric.

c.reason: Minus 8% lies inside the band. The mean ratio test is two-sided, so a negative value is judged on its absolute size, and 8% is below 10%.

d.reason: 22% exceeds the 20% ceiling on the variance ratio. This is a failure.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the trap for a candidate who has memorised "10%" without the plus-or-minus and therefore reads any negative value as a breach; the mean ratio band is two-sided while the variance ratio ceiling is one-sided. Option (b) is the trap for a candidate with the two thresholds transposed, since 18% would fail against a 10% ceiling. A variance ratio is naturally the larger number, so 20% goes with variance and 10% with the mean.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: Regulatory auditors are conducting an annual review of a trading desk's model compliance. Over the past 12 months they find that the $\text{Mean}(U)/\text{SD}(V)$ ratio exceeded plus 11% on three occasions and fell below minus 12% on two further occasions, and that the $\text{Var}(U)/\text{Var}(V)$ ratio exceeded 20% on four occasions, peaking at 28%. The desk maintained positive profit and loss throughout. What is the most likely regulatory outcome?

options.text: The internal model remains valid, since the desk was profitable throughout the period.
A capital surcharge is applied but the desk continues to use its internal model.
The desk must capitalise its positions using the standardised approach.
Conditional approval is granted pending further supervisory review, since neither metric failed on more than four occasions.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the count-based consequence of repeated profit and loss attribution failures, and the irrelevance of realised profitability to model validity.

Step 1. Count the breaches against each threshold.

| Metric | Threshold | Breaches observed |
|---|---|---|
| $\text{Mean}(U)/\text{SD}(V)$ | within $\pm10\%$ | 5 (three above plus 11%, two below minus 12%) |
| $\text{Var}(U)/\text{Var}(V)$ | must not exceed 20% | 4 (peaking at 28%) |

Step 2. Apply the rule: where four or more instances occur within a 12-month period in which the 10% or 20% conditions are broken, the desk must use the standardised approach. Both metrics reach that count independently, so the outcome is not marginal.

Step 3. Dispose of the profitability point, which is a deliberate distraction. The test measures whether the model explains the desk's outcomes. A desk can be highly profitable while running a model that fails to attribute that profit to the risk factors it claims to measure; unexplained profit is exactly as diagnostic of model failure as unexplained loss, which is why the mean ratio band is two-sided.

a.reason: Profitability is not a criterion anywhere in the rule. The mean ratio test is two-sided precisely because unexplained gains signal model failure just as unexplained losses do.

b.reason: A capital surcharge with continued model use is not the consequence specified for repeated profit and loss attribution failure under this framework. The consequence is a move to the standardised approach; the wrong remedy has been attached to the trigger.

c.reason: Five mean ratio breaches and four variance ratio breaches, either count sufficient to trigger the requirement.

d.reason: The premise fails on both metrics and on the rule. The mean ratio failed five times and the variance ratio four times, and the threshold is four or more, not more than four.

trap.explanation: Option (d) fails on an off-by-one reading of the condition, since the rule is "four or more", so exactly four is a breach rather than a near miss. Option (a) is the profitability distraction and is the one most likely to be selected under time pressure, because the stem volunteers the fact and invites its use; a volunteered fact in a stem is as often a red herring as an input.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: Basel II.5 introduced the incremental risk charge to prevent banks from reducing their capital requirement by booking a credit-dependent instrument in the trading book rather than the banking book. How does the FRTB address credit trades?

options.text: The FRTB makes no change to the incremental risk charge.

The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which recognises jump-to-default risk and mandates the inclusion of equity products.
The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from downgrade risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which explicitly excludes equity products.
The FRTB retains the IRC but recalibrates it to a 10-day, 97.5% confidence expected shortfall, consistent with the market risk measure.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the FRTB decomposition of credit exposure into two risks, and the replacement of the IRC by the DRC including the extension to equity.

The FRTB distinguishes two types of credit risk exposure to a company:

| Risk | Definition | How it is capitalised under the IMA |
|---|---|---|
| Credit spread risk | The risk that the company's credit spread changes, causing the mark-to-market value of the instrument to change | Handled like any other market risk inside the expected shortfall, with liquidity horizons from 20 to 120 days |
| Jump-to-default risk | The risk that the company defaults, producing an immediate loss or gain | Handled like default risk in the banking book: a VaR calculation with a one-year horizon and a 99.9% confidence level |

The IRC of Basel II.5 is replaced by the default risk charge. Two features are commonly tested: it recognises jump-to-default risk explicitly, and it mandates the inclusion of equity products, which the IRC did not cover. Including equity is logical once default is the organising concept, because a default drives the equity claim to zero just as surely as it impairs the debt claim.

Jump-to-default is distinct from downgrade risk. A downgrade is a migration event that moves the credit spread and is therefore captured inside credit spread risk. Jump-to-default is the discrete default event itself.

a.reason: The IRC does not survive the FRTB; it is replaced by the DRC. Asserting no change contradicts the central reform to credit treatment.

b.reason: Correct pair of risks, correct replacement, and correct on the extension to equity.

c.reason: Two defects. The second risk is jump-to-default, not downgrade; downgrade is a migration event captured within credit spread risk, and it is the near neighbour being substituted in. And the DRC includes equity products rather than excluding them.

d.reason: The IRC is not retained, and jump-to-default is not capitalised on the market risk calibration. It keeps the banking book calibration of one year at 99.9%, not the 10-day 97.5% market risk parameters, precisely because default is not a market risk phenomenon on a 10-day scale.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is built from two separate corruptions, either of which alone might be missed: the downgrade-versus-jump-to-default substitution is the subtler, since downgrade is a real credit risk concept that sounds like it belongs, and the equity point is reversed from included to excluded. Option (d) is the calibration trap, since jump-to-default keeps the banking book parameters rather than the market risk ones.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
questions.question: A bank is determining which of its exposures may be capitalised under the internal models approach. Which of the following correctly states the FRTB treatment of securitisation exposures?

options.text: Securitisation exposures may be capitalised under the internal models approach provided the bank's model has been approved for the correlation trading portfolio.
Securitisation exposures may be capitalised under the internal models approach, but with a liquidity horizon floor of 120 days.
Securitisation exposures are exempt from market risk capital and attract credit risk capital in the banking book instead.

Securitisation exposures must be capitalised under the STANDARDISED approach, because the internal models banks developed for these exposures under the earlier comprehensive risk measure differed widely from one another.

questions.solution:
Concept tested: the removal of internal models from securitisations, and the model-dispersion rationale behind it.

Under the FRTB, banks must use the standardised approach for securitisations; internal models are not available for these exposures at all.

The rationale is a model risk argument rather than a market risk argument. The pre-FRTB framework addressed securitisation risk through the comprehensive risk measure charge, which permitted banks to use their own models subject to supervisory oversight and approval. In practice the models banks built differed widely from one another, so that broadly similar exposures attracted materially different capital depending on whose model was used. That dispersion is unacceptable in a framework whose purpose includes comparability across institutions, so the FRTB disallowed internal models for securitisations entirely.

The consequence is that within the standardised approach the sensitivities-based method carries separate credit spread risk classes for securitisation exposures, split between those inside the correlation trading portfolio and those outside it.

a.reason: Model approval for the correlation trading portfolio does not unlock internal models for securitisations. The CTP is itself a securitisation category and is likewise capitalised under the standardised approach, so the stated condition cannot exist.

b.reason: There is no internal models route for securitisations to which a liquidity horizon floor could attach. The 120-day figure is the longest liquidity horizon in the schedule, borrowed from elsewhere to lend false specificity.

c.reason: Securitisation exposures held with trading intent remain in the trading book and attract market risk capital. What is removed is the choice of approach, not the applicability of the market risk framework, so the exposure has been assigned to the wrong regime.

d.reason: Standardised approach mandatory, with model dispersion under the comprehensive risk measure as the stated reason.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (b) both concede the right general direction, that securitisations are treated more harshly, while preserving an internal models route that does not exist. Partial concession is a standard way to build a distractor that survives a quick read; the rule is absolute, no internal models for securitisations.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on implied volatility
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a US bank is checking a dealer quote for no-arbitrage consistency. The spot value of a foreign currency is USD 0.5500. The continuously compounded risk-free rate is 4.0% per annum in the United States and 8.0% per annum in the foreign country. A one-year European call on the foreign currency struck at USD 0.5700 trades at USD 0.0325, and its implied volatility is 14.5% per annum. Applying put-call parity with the foreign risk-free rate in the role of the dividend yield $q$, which is nearest to the no-arbitrage value of the corresponding European put?
questions.solution:
Put-call parity for a currency option, where the foreign risk-free rate plays the role of a continuous dividend yield. The stated implied volatility is a distraction and is not needed.

Put-call parity for an asset paying a continuous yield $q$:

$$p + S_0 e^{-qT} = c + Ke^{-rT} \quad\Rightarrow\quad p = c + Ke^{-rT} - S_0 e^{-qT}$$

Assign each rate to its correct leg. The domestic rate $r$ discounts the strike, because the strike is a domestic-currency cash flow. The foreign rate $q$ discounts the spot, because holding the foreign currency earns the foreign rate.

$$Ke^{-rT} = 0.5700 \times e^{-0.04\times1} = 0.5700 \times 0.960789 = 0.547650$$
$$S_0 e^{-qT} = 0.5500 \times e^{-0.08\times1} = 0.5500 \times 0.923116 = 0.507714$$
$$p = 0.0325 + 0.547650 - 0.507714 = 0.072436$$

The put is worth approximately USD 0.0724. The implied volatility of 14.5% is not required and must not be used: parity is a no-arbitrage identity holding independently of any pricing model, and consistency with the call's 14.5% is guaranteed automatically by the equality of call and put implied volatility.

a.reason: USD 0.0302 swaps the two rates, discounting the strike at 8% and the spot at 4%: $0.0325+0.5700(0.923116)-0.5500(0.960789)=0.0302$. Each rate has been assigned to the wrong leg.

b.reason: USD 0.0525 $=0.0325+0.5700-0.5500$, dropping both discount factors and applying undiscounted parity.

c.reason: USD 0.0724, computed above.

d.reason: USD 0.0948 $=0.0325+0.5700-0.507714$, which discounts the spot but drops the discount factor on the strike.

trap.explanation: The real trap is time rather than arithmetic: the stated 14.5% implied volatility invites a full Black-Scholes computation that is unnecessary, since parity alone answers the question. The secondary trap is rate assignment, since the two rates are structurally close enough to be swapped without the answer looking absurd.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on implied volatility
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: An analyst estimates a stock's volatility at 34.0% per annum and uses that estimate in BSM to value a European call, obtaining a model price of USD 6.95. The call actually trades at USD 7.23. Using the same 34.0% volatility, he then values a European put on the same stock with the same strike and the same maturity, obtaining a BSM model price of USD 5.12. Which is nearest to the likely market price of the put?

options.text: USD 4.84
USD 5.12
USD 5.33
USD 5.40

questions.solution:
The dollar pricing error of BSM is identical for a European call and a European put that share a strike and a maturity.

From put-call parity applied to both model and market prices, the pricing errors must be equal:

$$c_{BSM} - c_{market} = p_{BSM} - p_{market}$$
$$6.95 - 7.23 = 5.12 - p_{market} \;\Rightarrow\; -0.28 = 5.12 - p_{market} \;\Rightarrow\; p_{market} = 5.12+0.28 = 5.40$$

Interpretation: BSM at 34.0% underprices the call by USD 0.28, and parity forces exactly the same USD 0.28 underpricing on the put. Equivalently, both options carry the same implied volatility and that implied volatility is above 34.0%, since the market pays more than the model says they are worth.

a.reason: USD 4.84 $=5.12-0.28$, subtracting the error instead of adding it. That would be the answer only if BSM had overpriced the call, that is, if the call had traded below USD 6.95.

b.reason: USD 5.12 is the BSM model price of the put, a genuine intermediate quantity of the correct working. Answering it means ignoring the pricing error entirely, which contradicts the evidence in the stem.

c.reason: USD 5.33 $=5.12\times(7.23/6.95)=5.12\times1.04029$. This applies the pricing error as a proportion rather than as a dollar amount. The parity identity is additive in dollars, not multiplicative.

d.reason: USD 5.40, computed above.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the subtlest and most instructive, because "the same pricing error" is naturally heard as "the same percentage error" when it is in fact the same dollar error. Writing the identity down before substituting, since the identity is stated in dollars, is the safeguard.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe volatility term structures and surfaces and their use in pricing
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question:
A financial engineer maintains the volatility surface below. The body of the table contains implied volatilities in percent computed from BSM. The rows are time to maturity and the columns are the ratio of strike to asset price, $K/S_0$. The asset price $S_0$ is USD 30.00. She needs to value an out-of-the-money call with a strike of USD 33.00 and a maturity of 4.0 years. Using bilinear interpolation, which is nearest to the implied volatility she should use?

| Maturity | $K/S=0.50$ | $K/S=0.75$ | $K/S=1.00$ | $K/S=1.25$ | $K/S=1.50$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 month | 36.9 | 28.9 | 20.9 | 14.9 | 15.2 |
| 3 months | 35.3 | 28.3 | 21.3 | 15.8 | 16.3 |
| 6 months | 32.9 | 26.9 | 20.9 | 16.0 | 16.8 |
| 1 year | 32.1 | 27.1 | 22.1 | 17.1 | 17.5 |
| 2 years | 29.8 | 25.8 | 21.8 | 16.8 | 18.0 |
| 5 years | 30.0 | 27.0 | 24.0 | 18.0 | 19.4 |
questions.solution:
Two-dimensional interpolation on a volatility surface, and the discipline of consuming both coordinates before answering.

Step 1. Locate the target cell: $K/S_0 = 33.00/30.00 = 1.10$, maturity $=4.0$ years. Neither coordinate lies on the grid; the target sits between columns 1.00 and 1.25 and between rows 2 years and 5 years.

Step 2. Interpolate along the strike dimension in each bracketing row. Weight on the upper column $=(1.10-1.00)/(1.25-1.00)=0.40$.
Row 2 years: $21.8+(16.8-21.8)\times0.40=21.8-2.00=19.80$.
Row 5 years: $24.0+(18.0-24.0)\times0.40=24.0-2.40=21.60$.

Step 3. Interpolate along the maturity dimension between those two results. Weight on the 5-year value $=(4-2)/(5-2)=0.6667$.

$$\text{implied volatility}=19.80+(21.60-19.80)\times0.6667=19.80+1.20=21.00$$

The engineer uses 21.00% as the volatility input to BSM or to a binomial tree.

a.reason: 17.60 rounds $K/S_0=1.10$ to the nearest grid column of 1.25 and then interpolates in maturity only: $16.8+(18.0-16.8)\times0.6667=17.60$. The strike interpolation has been dropped entirely.

b.reason: 19.80 is a genuine mid-calculation value, the interpolated value at [2 years, 1.10], produced by stopping after step 2. This is the classic case of computing correctly and answering the wrong question.

c.reason: 21.00, computed above.

d.reason: 23.27 interpolates in maturity only at the at-the-money column: $21.8+(24.0-21.8)\times0.6667=23.27$. It drops the strike interpolation in the opposite direction from (a).

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the intended kill, because it catches candidates who complete the harder half of the work and stop. Writing both target coordinates down first, then verifying both have been consumed before selecting, is the safeguard; options (a) and (d) are the two ways of doing only the easy half.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe volatility term structures and surfaces and their use in pricing | Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a smile
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question:
A stock trades at USD 50.00 and the risk-free rate is 3.0% per annum. For a series of European options with three months to maturity, observed market prices and the implied volatilities they generate are shown below. The market put price at the USD 46.00 strike has been omitted.

| Strike | Market call | Market put | Implied volatility |
|---|---|---|---|
| USD 42.00 | 9.02 | 0.70 | 36.6% |
| USD 44.00 | 8.32 | 1.99 | 47.9% |
| USD 46.00 | 7.64 | omitted | 54.5% |
| USD 48.00 | 7.05 | 4.69 | 59.7% |
| USD 50.00 | 6.50 | 6.13 | 63.8% |
| USD 52.00 | 5.31 | 6.92 | 60.2% |
| USD 54.00 | 4.17 | 7.77 | 56.3% |
| USD 56.00 | 3.09 | 8.68 | 51.8% |
| USD 58.00 | 1.69 | 9.26 | 42.1% |

Which of the following is correct?

options.text: The market price of the put is USD 3.30, and this is LOWER than the BSM model price computed with the at-the-money volatility of 63.8%.
The market price of the put is USD 3.30, and this is HIGHER than the BSM model price computed with the at-the-money volatility of 63.8%.
The market price of the put is USD 4.13, and this is LOWER than the BSM model price computed with the at-the-money volatility of 63.8%.
The market price of the put is USD 4.13, and this is EQUAL to the BSM model price computed with the at-the-money volatility of 63.8%.

questions.solution:
Recovering a missing market price by put-call parity, then reading the direction of the mispricing from the frown shape of the surface. A two-part conjunction item.

Part 1. Recover the market put price by put-call parity, using the observed market call at the same strike; no volatility is required.

$$p = c + Ke^{-rT} - S_0, \qquad Ke^{-rT} = 46.00\times e^{-0.03\times0.25} = 46.00\times0.992528 = 45.65629$$
$$p = 7.64 + 45.65629 - 50.00 = 3.2963 \approx \text{USD } 3.30$$

Part 2. Determine the direction relative to the model price at 63.8%. The fast route is the shape of the curve: implied volatility peaks at 63.8% at the money and falls away on both sides, reaching 36.6% at the far left and 42.1% at the far right, a frown. The USD 46.00 strike carries 54.5%, below the at-the-money 63.8%. Since vega is positive, pricing that option with the higher at-the-money volatility must produce a higher price than the market pays, so the market price is lower.

Confirming by direct computation with $S=50.00$, $K=46.00$, $r=0.03$, $T=0.25$, $\sigma=0.638$:

$$d_1=\frac{\ln(50/46)+(0.03+0.638^2/2)\times0.25}{0.638\sqrt{0.25}}=\frac{0.083382+0.058381}{0.319}=0.4444,\quad d_2=0.4444-0.319=0.1254$$
$$N(-d_1)=0.3284,\quad N(-d_2)=0.4501$$
$$p_{model} = 45.65629\times0.4501 - 50.00\times0.3284 = 20.549-16.421 = 4.13$$

Model price USD 4.13 against market price USD 3.30: the market price is lower, confirming Part 2.

a.reason: USD 3.30 from parity, and lower than the USD 4.13 model price because the strike's own implied volatility of 54.5% is below the at-the-money 63.8%.

b.reason: Correct price, wrong direction. This is what results from reading the curve as a smile rather than a frown, that is, from assuming the at-the-money implied volatility is the lowest point rather than the highest.

c.reason: USD 4.13 is the model price computed at the at-the-money volatility, not the market price. It is a real quantity in the correct working that answers a different question, and it is the most dangerous option on the page because the direction half happens to be correct.

d.reason: Both halves fail. USD 4.13 is again the model price rather than the market price, and the two are not equal; equality would require the USD 46.00 strike to carry the same implied volatility as the at-the-money strike, which the table contradicts at 54.5% against 63.8%.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the intended kill: a candidate who computes the BSM price at 63.8% and stops has produced USD 4.13 and will read it as "the price of the put", when the stem asks for the market price, recovered from parity using the observed call and never requiring a volatility. This is also the only item in this set where the surface is a frown rather than an equity skew, which is precisely why the direction half catches people.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question:
Assuming returns are normally distributed, expected shortfall can be computed without a standard normal density lookup using the expression below, in which $X$ is the confidence level and $Y$ is the standard normal quantile that has probability $(1-X)$ of being exceeded. If the daily mean return is $+1.0\%$ and the daily standard deviation is $5.0\%$, which is nearest to the daily 97.5% expected shortfall expressed as a loss?

$$ES = -\mu + \sigma \times \frac{\exp(-Y^2/2)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,(1-X)}$$
questions.solution:
Numerical computation of normal expected shortfall, and the sign convention when the stated mean is a positive expected return but the answer is required as a loss.

Step 1. Identify the quantile. For $X=97.5\%$, the standard normal point with 2.5% probability of being exceeded is $Y=1.960$.

Step 2. Evaluate the tail multiplier.

$$\exp(-Y^2/2)=\exp(-1.960^2/2)=\exp(-1.9208)=0.146373$$
$$\sqrt{2\pi}\times(1-X)=2.506628\times0.025=0.0626657$$
$$\text{multiplier}=0.146373/0.0626657=2.3358$$

Step 3. Apply the sign convention. The stated mean of $+1.0\%$ is an expected profit, so it reduces the expected loss in the tail.

$$ES = -1.0\%+5.0\%\times2.3358 = -1.0\%+11.679\% = 10.679\%$$

Shortcut: under normality the 97.5% expected shortfall is almost exactly the 99% VaR, whose multiplier is 2.326. Using 2.326 gives $-1.0\%+11.63\%=10.63\%$, which selects the same option in a fraction of the time and requires no density evaluation.

a.reason: 4.00% $=5.0\%-1.0\%$, a one standard deviation move net of the mean. The tail multiplier has been dropped entirely.

b.reason: 7.22% $=-1.0\%+5.0\%\times1.645$, substituting the 95% VaR deviate. Wrong confidence level and wrong measure.

c.reason: 8.80% $=-1.0\%+5.0\%\times1.960$. This is the 97.5% value at risk, not the expected shortfall. It uses $Y$ itself as the multiplier instead of feeding $Y$ into the ES expression, stopping one step early on a quantity that genuinely appears in the working.

d.reason: 10.68%, computed above.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the intended kill: $Y=1.960$ is genuinely required, so a candidate who computes it and multiplies immediately, stopping one step early, produces a real number that answers a different question. The sign convention is the second trap: a positive mean return is subtracted when the answer is expressed as a loss.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
questions.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
questions.question: Consider an exposure with a value of USD 30.0 million. Expressed in loss-positive format, its expected loss is 4.0% with a volatility of 15.0%; that is, the mean of the loss distribution is $+4.0\%$ and $\sigma$ is 15.0%. The exposure happens to be normally distributed. Which is nearest to the single-period 97.5% expected shortfall?

options.text: USD 9.32 million
USD 10.02 million
USD 11.72 million
USD 13.19 million

questions.solution:
Applying normal expected shortfall to an exposure in loss-positive format, where the mean is added rather than subtracted.

Note the format first. The stem states the distribution in loss-positive format, so the stated mean of $+4.0\%$ is an expected loss. It therefore adds to the tail loss, the opposite of the convention used when the mean is a positive return.

$$ES_{97.5\%} = \mu + \sigma\times2.3378 = 4.0\%+15.0\%\times2.3378 = 4.0\%+35.067\% = 39.067\%$$
$$ES_{\text{currency}} = \text{USD }30.0\text{ million}\times39.067\% = \text{USD }11.72\text{ million}$$

Using the shortcut multiplier of 2.326, the 99% VaR equivalent, gives $4.0\%+34.90\%=38.90\%$ and USD 11.67 million, which selects the same option.

a.reason: USD 9.32 million $=30.0\times(15.0\%\times2.3378-4.0\%)$. This subtracts the mean instead of adding it, which is correct only when the mean is a positive return in profit-positive format. Here the format is loss-positive.

b.reason: USD 10.02 million $=30.0\times(4.0\%+15.0\%\times1.960)$. This is the 97.5% value at risk, obtained by stopping at the quantile rather than proceeding to the expected shortfall multiplier.

c.reason: USD 11.72 million, computed above.

d.reason: USD 13.19 million $=30.0\times(4.0\%+15.0\%\times2.6650)$, where 2.6650 is the 99% expected shortfall multiplier. Right measure, wrong confidence level, so the twin parameter has been substituted.

trap.explanation: The sign of the mean is the whole question, and this item uses the opposite convention from its companion question: same formula, opposite format. Reading the format label before writing anything down is the safeguard: a positive return is subtracted, a positive expected loss is added. Options (b) and (d) then police the two ways of picking the wrong multiplier, right level with wrong measure, versus right measure with wrong level.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a normal rate tree, with and without drift
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: An analyst is modelling short-term interest rates assuming rates are normally distributed with NO drift. The current short-term rate is 7.18%, the time interval is three months (3/12 of a year), and volatility is 118 basis points per year. Over the three months the random variable $dw$ takes the value 0.18. What are the change in the short-term rate and the level of the short-term rate after three months?

options.text: Change 0.2124%; level 7.3924%
Change 0.0531%; level 7.2331%
Change 0.2124%; level 6.9676%
Change 0.4248%; level 7.6048%

questions.solution:
Model 1 is the simplest term structure model. It simulates a single step of the normally distributed, no-drift short-rate process. It has no drift and constant annualised basis-point volatility:

$$dr = \sigma\, dw$$

where $dr$ is the change in the short rate over the interval, $\sigma$ is the annualised basis-point volatility, and $dw$ is a normally distributed random variable with mean 0 and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

$\sigma = 118$ basis points $= 1.18\%$

$dr = 1.18\% \times 0.18 = 0.2124\%$

$r_{new} = 7.18\% + 0.2124\% = 7.3924\%$

The rate rises by about 21 basis points to 7.3924%. Note carefully that $dt = 3/12$ does NOT appear anywhere in the substitution. Under Model 1 the realised change is $\sigma$ multiplied by the REALISED value of $dw$. The time interval enters only through the DISTRIBUTION of $dw$, whose standard deviation is $\sqrt{dt} = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$. Since the stem hands you the realised value of $dw$ directly, $dt$ is not needed.

a.reason: $dr = 1.18\% \times 0.18 = 0.2124\%$, added to the starting rate of 7.18%.

b.reason: $0.0531\% = 1.18\% \times 0.18 \times 0.25$, which multiplies by $dt$ as though the volatility term needed time scaling. It does not; the time scaling is already inside the realised $dw$.

c.reason: The magnitude of the change is right but the sign is reversed. $dw = +0.18$ is positive, so the rate RISES.

d.reason: $0.4248\% = 1.18\% \times 0.18 \times 2$, which double counts. There is no factor of two in Model 1.

trap.explanation: The time interval is a red herring in this specific construction, and option (b) exists to punish anyone who feels obliged to use every number in the stem. Under Model 1 with a realised $dw$ supplied, $dr = \sigma \times dw$ and nothing else; if instead the question had asked for the standard deviation of the change, $dt$ would matter and the answer would be $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$. Read whether you are asked for a realised change or a distributional property.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a normal rate tree, with and without drift
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: In Model 1 the short-term rate is the single factor and there is no drift. If the short-term rate rises by 20 basis points, what is the effect on the term structure?

options.text: Volatility across the term structure rises by 20 basis points.
Convexity rises by 20 basis points.
Only rates at the short end rise; long rates are unaffected because Model 1 has no drift.
Rates across the entire term structure rise by 20 basis points, a parallel shift.

questions.solution:
Model 1 has exactly one source of uncertainty, the short-term rate, and constant volatility:

$$dr = \sigma\, dw$$

Because the short rate is the ONLY factor, every spot and forward rate in the model is a deterministic function of it. A shift in the short rate therefore feeds through to the whole curve. With no drift and no mean reversion there is nothing to dampen the shock as maturity lengthens, so the pass-through is one for one and the shift is PARALLEL. This is precisely where the model's effectiveness breaks down:

| Model 1 property | Empirical reality |
|---|---|
