| All rate changes are perfectly correlated; only parallel shifts occur | The curve steepens, flattens and twists; long rates move less than short rates |
| Volatility is the same at every maturity | The term structure of volatility is humped, not flat |
| The term structure is very slightly downward sloping, driven only by convexity | Curves are usually upward sloping, reflecting a risk premium |
| Rates can drift arbitrarily far from any level, including below zero | Rates are bounded in practice and revert toward a level |

a.reason: Volatility in Model 1 is the constant parameter $\sigma$. It is an input, not an output, and it does not respond to the level of the rate.

b.reason: Convexity is a property of the price-to-yield relationship of a bond and is measured in units of time squared. It is not measured in basis points and does not shift with the short rate.

c.reason: This describes mean reversion, which Model 1 does not contain. In a mean-reverting model a shock to the short rate decays with maturity and long rates move less than one for one. That is the Vasicek result, not Model 1.

d.reason: One factor with no drift and no mean reversion produces a parallel shift of the entire term structure.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the sibling swap and is the strongest distractor because the described behaviour, long rates moving less than short rates, is both empirically correct AND a real model property, just of a different model. Model 1 has no mechanism to produce it. Ask what the model contains, not what markets do. Options (a) and (b) are unit errors: neither volatility nor convexity is denominated in a way that lets it move by 20 basis points.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a normal rate tree, with and without drift
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: Model 2 adds a constant drift to Model 1 and is written as $dr = \lambda\, dt + \sigma\, dw$. Given $r(0) = 6.138\%$, $\lambda = 0.239\%$ per year and $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year, what are the drift of the rate and the standard deviation of the rate change, both expressed PER MONTH?

options.text: Drift 0.01992%; standard deviation 0.3464%
Drift 0.01992%; standard deviation 0.1000%
Drift 0.2390%; standard deviation 0.3464%
Drift 0.2390%; standard deviation 0.1000%

questions.solution:
Model 2 is Model 1 plus a constant drift term:

$$dr = \lambda\, dt + \sigma\, dw$$

The two terms scale with time in DIFFERENT ways, and that is the whole question.

drift over the interval $= \lambda \times dt$

standard deviation over the interval $= \sigma \times \sqrt{dt}$

With $dt = 1/12$ of a year:

drift $= 0.239\% \times (1/12) = 0.01992\%$ per month

standard deviation $= 1.20\% \times \sqrt{1/12} = 1.20\% \times 0.288675 = 0.3464\%$ per month

Interpretation: the rate is expected to rise by about 2 basis points per month, while the one standard deviation dispersion around that expectation is about 35 basis points. Uncertainty dominates drift at short horizons. Because drift grows with $t$ and dispersion only with $\sqrt{t}$, drift eventually dominates at long horizons, which is exactly why a constant positive drift in Model 2 produces an unrealistically steep curve at long maturities.

a.reason: $\lambda \times dt$ for the drift, $\sigma \times \sqrt{dt}$ for the standard deviation.

b.reason: The drift is right but the standard deviation has been scaled by $dt$ rather than $\sqrt{dt}$: $1.20\% \times (1/12) = 0.1000\%$. This is the square-root-of-time error, and it understates dispersion severely.

c.reason: The standard deviation is right but the drift has not been scaled at all, leaving the annual figure of 0.239% as though it were monthly.

d.reason: Both errors at once: an unscaled annual drift and a linearly scaled standard deviation.

trap.explanation: The option set is a deliberate two-by-two grid, so guessing on either half alone leaves a fifty per cent chance of failing. The single fact that resolves it is that drift is linear in time while standard deviation is linear in the square root of time. Write $dt$ and $\sqrt{dt}$ side by side before substituting anything.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a normal rate tree, with and without drift
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: Under Model 2 the current short-term rate is 5.26%, annual volatility is 115 basis points, the annual drift is 0.25%, and the interval is one month. One month passes and the random variable $dw$ takes the value 0.25. What is the short-term rate after one month?
questions.solution:
Apply the Model 2 dynamics term by term.

$$dr = \lambda\, dt + \sigma\, dw$$

drift term $= 0.25\% \times (1/12) = 0.020833\%$

random term $= 1.15\% \times 0.25 = 0.287500\%$

$dr = 0.020833\% + 0.287500\% = 0.308333\%$

$r_{new} = 5.26\% + 0.308333\% = 5.5683\%$

The rate after one month is approximately 5.5683%. Note how small the drift contribution is relative to the random contribution over a one-month step: about 2 basis points against about 29. Over a single short step, Model 2 and Model 1 are nearly indistinguishable, which is why the distractor at (b) is only 21 basis points away from the correct answer.

a.reason: 0.3083% is the CHANGE in the rate, not the level. It is a genuine intermediate result of the correct calculation and answers a different question.

b.reason: $5.5475\% = 5.26\% + 0.2875\%$, which omits the drift term entirely and therefore solves the problem as if it were Model 1. This is the sibling swap between the two models.

c.reason: 5.5683%, computed above.

d.reason: $5.7975\% = 5.26\% + 0.25\% + 0.2875\%$, which adds the ANNUAL drift without multiplying by $dt$. This is the same scaling error tested with Model 2 drift, here expressed as a level.

trap.explanation: Three named errors, one per distractor: the intermediate result at (a), the dropped drift term at (b), and the unscaled drift at (d). Option (a) is the most dangerous because the number is real and appears in your own working. Underline the word asking for a LEVEL or a CHANGE before you start.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a normal rate tree, with and without drift
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: An analyst is building a binomial tree for the short-term rate under Model 1, in which rates are normally distributed with no drift. The current short rate is 4.00%, the annualised volatility is 1.20%, and each step of the tree is three months. Up and down moves are equally likely. Which is the HIGHEST short rate in the tree after TWO steps?
questions.solution:
Under Model 1 with no drift, the tree steps up or down from each node by one standard deviation of the change over the step, with equal risk-neutral probabilities of one half:

step size $= \sigma \times \sqrt{dt}$

step size $= 1.20\% \times \sqrt{0.25} = 1.20\% \times 0.50 = 0.60\%$

Building outward from $r(0) = 4.00\%$:

| Path | Node value |
|---|---|
| Date 0 | 4.00% |
| Up (Date 1) | 4.60% |
| Up-Up (Date 2) | 5.20% |
| Middle (Date 2) | 4.00% |
| Down (Date 1) | 3.40% |
| Down-Down (Date 2) | 2.80% |

The highest rate after two steps is $4.00\% + 2 \times 0.60\% = 5.20\%$.

Two structural features are worth naming. The tree RECOMBINES, because an up move followed by a down move returns exactly to 4.00%, which keeps the number of nodes linear rather than exponential in the number of steps. And the tree is SYMMETRIC about the starting rate, which is the visual signature of a model with zero drift.

a.reason: 4.60% is the up node after ONE step. It is an intermediate result, produced by stopping one step short.

b.reason: $4.85\% = 4.00\% + 1.20\% \times \sqrt{0.5}$, which treats the six months as a SINGLE step rather than two three-month steps. That correctly scales volatility to six months but discards the tree structure, and it understates the extreme node because two steps of $\sqrt{0.25}$ exceed one step of $\sqrt{0.50}$.

d.reason: $6.40\% = 4.00\% + 2 \times 1.20\%$, which applies the ANNUAL volatility at each step without scaling by $\sqrt{dt}$.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is the missing $\sqrt{dt}$, the single most common slip in tree construction. Option (b) is subtler: scaling to the terminal horizon in one step is not the same as taking two steps, because the extreme path in a two-step tree accumulates $2\sigma\sqrt{dt}$, which is larger than $\sigma\sqrt{2\,dt}$. Trees widen linearly in the number of steps while the distribution widens with the square root; that gap is exactly the tail of the binomial distribution.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: Term structure models in which the terminal distribution of rates is normal are called Gaussian models. A known limitation is that the modelled short rate can become negative. Which statement best characterises the economic objection to negative short-term rates?

options.text: Negative rates are attractive to lenders because they eliminate lending risk.
Negative short-term rates affect neither borrowers nor lenders, because rates revert to positive levels in the long run.
Negative rates cannot arise in practice because central banks are legally prohibited from setting a policy rate below zero.
Individuals will generally not lend at a negative rate, because they can instead hold cash and earn zero.

questions.solution:
The objection is an arbitrage argument, not a legal one. Physical currency is a zero-coupon, zero-yield instrument available to anyone. If lending at a negative rate means being repaid less than the amount lent, an individual can simply hold the cash instead and be repaid exactly what they started with. That dominates the negative-rate loan, so no such loan should occur. This is the ZERO LOWER BOUND.

Two qualifications matter, and both are examinable. The bound is not absolute: holding large quantities of physical cash has real costs including storage, insurance and transport, so the true bound is slightly below zero rather than exactly at zero. Institutions facing those costs, and institutions obliged to hold central bank reserves, have accepted negative rates in practice, and negative policy rates have been observed in Japan, Switzerland and the euro area.

The word INDIVIDUALS is doing work in the correct option. The argument applies most cleanly to an agent who can costlessly substitute into cash. Central banks and governments can and do transact at negative rates under specific policy conditions.

a.reason: A negative rate means the lender receives back less than was lent, which reduces return. It is unattractive, not attractive. The phrase 'zero lending risk' also confuses the rate paid with credit risk, which are unrelated.

b.reason: Rates that are negative today affect decisions today, regardless of where they settle later. The statement also concedes the modelling problem without addressing it: the issue is that a Gaussian model assigns positive probability to negative rates at every horizon.

c.reason: There is no such legal prohibition, and the claim is empirically false: several major central banks have set negative policy rates. The bound is economic and approximate, not legal and absolute.

d.reason: The cash alternative is what creates the bound.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the absolute-claim trap and is made attractive by the fact that the zero lower bound is often taught as though it were a hard constraint. It is a soft, cost-based bound that has been breached repeatedly since 2014. Option (a) is a straight polarity flip. Hold the mechanism, which is the cash substitute, rather than the slogan.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: One method of handling negative rates is to construct an interest rate tree with the desired distribution and then set any negative rates in that tree to zero. Under this method, how are the rates in the ORIGINAL tree and the rates in the ADJUSTED tree respectively described?

options.text: Original rates are the observed rates; adjusted rates are the shadow rates.
Original rates are the expected rates; adjusted rates are the volatile market rates.
Original rates are the short-term rates; adjusted rates are the forward rates.
Original rates are the shadow rates; adjusted rates are the observed rates.

questions.solution:
The method proceeds in two stages. First, build the tree exactly as the model specifies, allowing rates to go wherever the distribution takes them, including below zero. Second, replace every negative rate with zero and use the adjusted tree for pricing.

| Tree | Name | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Original, unadjusted | SHADOW rates | What the rate 'would be' if the cash alternative did not exist. May be negative. |
| Adjusted, floored at zero | OBSERVED rates | What can actually be transacted at, and what is used to discount cash flows. |

The naming follows the economics: the shadow rate is unobservable and hypothetical, while the floored rate is the one you can see in the market. Get the direction wrong and the whole concept inverts.

The method has a side effect that the LO expects you to know: flooring truncates the left tail of the distribution, which RAISES the mean of the modelled rate and REDUCES its volatility relative to the unadjusted model. The adjusted tree is therefore no longer the distribution you specified.

a.reason: Reversed. The observable, transactable rates are the ADJUSTED ones. Calling the unadjusted negative rates 'observed' contradicts the reason they are being adjusted.

b.reason: Neither label is used in this context. 'Expected rates' and 'volatile market rates' are not the terminology of the flooring method.

c.reason: Forward rates are a different object entirely, derived from the term structure rather than produced by flooring a tree.

d.reason: Shadow rates before the floor, observed rates after it.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is a pure polarity flip on the naming, and it is the only distractor a prepared candidate can realistically fall for. Anchor the direction with the everyday meaning of the word: a shadow is the thing you cannot touch, so shadow rates are the hypothetical ones. What you observe is what you can actually trade at, which is the floored series.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: A model validation analyst is documenting the approaches available for preventing negative short-term rates in a term structure model. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment?

options.text: Flooring a normally distributed tree at zero leaves the mean and volatility of the modelled rate unchanged, which is why it is preferred to changing the distribution.
The only available method is to adopt a distribution that cannot go negative, such as a lognormal or square-root process, because flooring a tree introduces arbitrage.

There are two methods: flooring a normally distributed tree at zero, and adopting a distribution that cannot produce negative rates. Flooring raises the mean and lowers the volatility of the modelled rate relative to the unadjusted model.
There are two methods, but both are unnecessary in practice, since observed nominal short rates have never been negative.

questions.solution:
Two families of solution exist, and the LO asks for methods in the plural.

| Method | How it works | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Floor the tree at zero | Build the tree from the chosen (normal) distribution, then replace negative nodes with zero. Original nodes are shadow rates; floored nodes are observed rates. | The realised distribution is no longer the one specified. Truncating the left tail RAISES the mean and LOWERS the volatility. |
| Change the distribution | Use a process that cannot go negative by construction, for example a lognormal process, or a square-root process in which basis-point volatility falls to zero as the rate approaches zero. | The rate distribution and the behaviour of volatility are no longer free choices; they are dictated by the functional form. |

The flooring side effect is the examinable nuance. Setting all negative draws to zero removes mass from the left tail and piles it at zero. Removing the lowest values raises the mean, and compressing the range reduces dispersion. So a model that was calibrated to a target volatility before flooring will exhibit LOWER volatility after it.

a.reason: Polarity error on the consequence. Truncation necessarily changes both moments: it raises the mean and lowers the volatility. That distortion is precisely the drawback of the flooring approach.

b.reason: Two defects. Flooring is a recognised method, so it is not 'the only' alternative; and flooring does not introduce arbitrage, it distorts the distribution.

c.reason: Both methods identified, with the correct direction of the flooring distortion.

d.reason: Empirically false. Negative nominal policy and market rates have been observed in Japan, Switzerland and the euro area, which is exactly why the modelling problem became practically important rather than merely theoretical.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the polarity trap and is tempting because 'we only changed the negative values, which were rare' feels like a small intervention. It is not: truncation is a systematic change to the distribution and it moves both moments in predictable directions. State the direction out loud, mean UP and volatility DOWN, before choosing.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Construct a short-term rate tree under the Ho-Lee model
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: An analyst constructs a short-rate tree under the Ho-Lee model, $dr = \lambda(t)\, dt + \sigma\, dw$. The current short rate is 5.00% and the annualised volatility is 1.20%. Each step is three months. The calibrated time-dependent drift is $\lambda(1) = 0.40\%$ per year over the first step and $\lambda(2) = 0.80\%$ per year over the second step. Which is the MIDDLE node of the tree after two steps?
questions.solution:
Ho-Lee is Model 2 with the constant drift replaced by a date-dependent drift, calibrated so that the model reproduces observed market bond prices:

$$dr = \lambda(t)\, dt + \sigma\, dw$$

Step 1. Compute the volatility step, which is constant across the tree:

$\sigma\sqrt{dt} = 1.20\% \times \sqrt{0.25} = 0.60\%$

Step 2. Compute the drift applied at each step, remembering to scale by $dt$:

first step: $\lambda(1) \times dt = 0.40\% \times 0.25 = 0.10\%$

second step: $\lambda(2) \times dt = 0.80\% \times 0.25 = 0.20\%$

Step 3. Build the tree. Every node at a given date receives the SAME drift increment; only the volatility term differs by path.

| Path | Node value |
|---|---|
| Date 0 | 5.00% |
| Up (Date 1) | 5.70% $= 5.00\% + 0.10\% + 0.60\%$ |
| Up-Up (Date 2) | 6.50% $= 5.70\% + 0.20\% + 0.60\%$ |
| Up-Down (Date 2) | 5.30% $= 5.70\% + 0.20\% - 0.60\%$ |
| Down (Date 1) | 4.50% $= 5.00\% + 0.10\% - 0.60\%$ |
| Down-Up (Date 2) | 5.30% $= 4.50\% + 0.20\% + 0.60\%$ |
| Down-Down (Date 2) | 4.10% $= 4.50\% + 0.20\% - 0.60\%$ |

The middle node is 5.30%, reached by both the up-down and the down-up paths, so the tree RECOMBINES: an up followed by a down cancels exactly because the drift increment at each date is identical across nodes and the volatility step is constant.

Cross-check without building the tree: the middle node equals the starting rate plus the cumulative drift, since the volatility terms cancel. That is $5.00\% + 0.10\% + 0.20\% = 5.30\%$.

a.reason: 5.00% is the middle node of a tree with NO drift, which would be Model 1. It omits both drift increments.

b.reason: 5.10% applies only the first period drift and omits the second. It is the middle node after ONE step in drift terms, an intermediate result.

d.reason: $6.20\% = 5.00\% + 0.40\% + 0.80\%$, adding the ANNUALISED drifts without multiplying each by $dt = 0.25$.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is the unscaled drift, the same error as elsewhere whenever lambda is quoted per year. Option (b) catches the candidate who notices that the drift changes by date and then applies only the first value. The fastest route to the middle node is the cross-check: volatility cancels along a recombining path, so the middle node is simply the start plus the sum of the scaled drifts. Use the full tree only when an outer node is asked for.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe uses of arbitrage-free models and assess fitting to market prices
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: A desk must choose between an arbitrage-free model and an equilibrium model. What is the principal USE of an arbitrage-free model?

options.text: Quoting prices on the basis of the credit standing of the issuing institution.
Determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.
Forecasting the level of the short-term rate over long horizons.
Quoting the prices of securities that are not actively traded, on the basis of the prices of more liquid securities.

questions.solution:
An arbitrage-free model is calibrated, through its time-dependent drift, to reproduce the observed prices of a set of liquid securities exactly. That single property determines both what the model is good for and what it is useless for.

| Purpose | Arbitrage-free model | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Price an illiquid security off liquid ones | APPROPRIATE | The model reproduces the liquid prices exactly, so the derived price is consistent with the instruments you would actually hedge with |
| Value and hedge derivatives for market making | APPROPRIATE | Hedges are executed in the liquid instruments whose prices the model matches |
| Judge whether market prices are fair | INAPPROPRIATE | The model ASSUMES the prices are correct, so it can never disagree with them |

The second use in the table is the one emphasised alongside the first: arbitrage-free models are used for valuing and hedging derivative securities, whether for making markets or for proprietary trading.

a.reason: Credit standing affects the price of a specific issuer's debt but is not what a term structure model is calibrated to or used for.

b.reason: This is the one thing an arbitrage-free model cannot do, because it takes market prices as an input rather than producing them as an output. Assessing fair value calls for an equilibrium model, whose prices come from economic assumptions and can therefore disagree with the market.

c.reason: The drift in an arbitrage-free model is a risk-neutral calibration parameter that bundles expectations with a risk premium. It is not a real-world forecast and should not be read as one.

d.reason: Relative pricing of illiquid instruments against liquid ones is the primary use.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the exact inversion of the model's logic and is the highest-yield distractor in this LO, because 'arbitrage-free' sounds like it should mean 'detects arbitrage'. It means the opposite: the model is constructed so that no arbitrage exists against the fitted prices, which requires assuming those prices are right. Bind the pair: arbitrage-free for RELATIVE pricing, equilibrium for FAIR value.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe uses of arbitrage-free models and assess fitting to market prices
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: A risk committee is reviewing a desk's use of an arbitrage-free term structure model that is calibrated to fit observed bond prices exactly. Which of the following is the most appropriate assessment of the fitting exercise?

options.text: An exact fit to market prices is always desirable, because any pricing error in the model would create an arbitrage opportunity against the desk.
An exact fit guarantees that the model will continue to price accurately as the term structure moves, because the calibration is re-derived at every node.
The quality of the fit is irrelevant, because the drift parameters are estimated from historical data rather than from current prices.

An exact fit means the model takes market prices as correct, so it cannot identify mispricing; and if the fit requires an implausible path for the drift, that is evidence that either the model or some of the fitted prices should be questioned.

questions.solution:
Fitting an arbitrage-free model to market prices carries two costs that a risk committee should understand.

Cost 1: the model surrenders any independent view on value. A model calibrated to reproduce a set of prices exactly will, by construction, agree with every one of those prices. If one of the fitted securities is mispriced, the model absorbs the mispricing into its drift and reports no error. An arbitrage-free model can therefore never tell you that the market is wrong. That is a design feature, not a defect, but it makes the model unsuitable for relative value assessment of the fitted instruments themselves.

Cost 2: an implausible calibrated drift is a diagnostic signal. Because the drift bundles expectations with a risk premium, it should trace an economically sensible path. If matching every observed price requires a drift that swings violently or implies expected rate paths no one holds, the sensible inference is that the model lacks a feature it needs, such as mean reversion or a second factor, or that some of the fitted prices are stale or unreliable. Forcing the fit anyway hides the problem inside a parameter.

Practical consequence: a desk should fit to a carefully chosen set of LIQUID instruments and then inspect the implied drift, rather than fitting to everything available and treating a perfect fit as proof of a good model.

a.reason: Confuses two different things. A model that disagrees with a market price does not create an arbitrage; it creates a TRADING VIEW, which may be right or wrong. Arbitrage requires a riskless profit, not a difference of opinion between a model and a screen.

b.reason: Fitting today's prices says nothing about tomorrow's. Arbitrage-free models generally require RECALIBRATION as the curve moves, and a model that must be refitted frequently and substantially is displaying instability rather than accuracy.

c.reason: Factually reversed. The defining feature of an arbitrage-free model is that its time-dependent drift is calibrated to CURRENT market prices. Estimation from historical data is characteristic of equilibrium models.

d.reason: Both costs correctly identified: no independent view on value, and an implausible drift path as a diagnostic.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the strongest distractor because it deploys the word 'arbitrage' in a setting where the word appears in the model's name, which creates a false sense of coherence. Keep the definitions apart: arbitrage-free describes internal consistency with fitted prices, not the detection of trading opportunities. Option (b) is the stability trap, and the tell is the word 'guarantees'.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: A time-dependent volatility function for the short rate can be written as $dr = \lambda(t)\, dt + \sigma(t)\, dw$. In this specification, on what does the volatility of the short rate depend?

options.text: On the level of the short rate itself.
On the volatility of the parameter sigma.
On time.
On changes in the market prices of the securities being fitted.

questions.solution:
Read the notation literally. The diffusion coefficient is written $\sigma(t)$, a function whose single argument is $t$. Volatility therefore depends on TIME and on nothing else.

Three distinctions follow, and each is contested by one of the distractors:

| Specification | Volatility depends on | Example model |
|---|---|---|
| $\sigma$ (constant) | nothing | Model 1, Model 2, Ho-Lee |
| $\sigma(t)$ | calendar time only, deterministically | Model 3, time-dependent volatility models |
| $\sigma \times f(r)$ | the LEVEL of the rate | square-root and lognormal processes |
| stochastic $\sigma$ | its own random process | stochastic volatility models |

The word DETERMINISTIC matters. $\sigma(t)$ is known in advance for every future date; it is not random. That is why these are called deterministic volatility functions, and it is what makes them tractable enough to be calibrated to a set of option prices.

a.reason: Volatility depending on the level of the rate is a different specification entirely, written with $r$ inside the diffusion term. In $\sigma(t)$ the rate does not appear.

b.reason: This describes stochastic volatility, in which $\sigma$ has its own random process. $\sigma(t)$ is deterministic: it varies with time but is known in advance.

c.reason: The argument of the function is $t$, so volatility is a deterministic function of time.

d.reason: Market prices are what the function is CALIBRATED TO, not what it depends on functionally. Confusing the calibration target with the argument of the function inverts the direction of the relationship.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the sibling swap toward level-dependent volatility, and option (b) is the sibling swap toward stochastic volatility. Both are real specifications from adjacent material. The discipline is mechanical: read what is inside the parentheses. If it is $t$, volatility depends on time; if it is $r$, on the rate level; if $\sigma$ has its own $dw$ term, it is stochastic.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: Deterministic volatility functions are used to match the market prices of caplets with different expiration dates, because a caplet's value depends on the distribution of the short rate at its expiry. At expiration, what does a caplet pay?

options.text: The difference between the short rate and the strike rate, if that difference is positive, on a notional amount.
The difference between the short rate and the strike rate, if that difference is negative, on a notional amount.
The strike rate on a notional amount, provided the strike rate has risen.
The short rate on a notional amount, regardless of the strike rate.

questions.solution:
A caplet is a call option on an interest rate. At expiry it pays:

$$\text{payoff} = \text{Notional} \times \max(r - K, 0) \times (\text{day count fraction})$$

where $r$ is the reference short rate at expiry and $K$ is the strike rate. The holder is compensated only when the rate exceeds the strike, which is what makes a caplet insurance against rising rates. A strip of caplets covering successive periods is a CAP.

The connection to the LO is the important part. The value of a caplet expiring at date $T$ depends on the DISTRIBUTION of the short rate at date $T$, and therefore on the volatility of the short rate between now and $T$. Caplets with different expiries therefore reveal information about volatility at different horizons. A model with a single constant $\sigma$ has only one degree of freedom and generally cannot match a whole strip of caplet prices. A model with $\sigma(t)$ has as many degrees of freedom as there are dates, so it CAN be fitted to them. That flexibility is the reason deterministic volatility functions exist.

a.reason: A caplet pays the positive part of the excess of the rate over the strike.

b.reason: Paying when the difference is NEGATIVE describes a FLOORLET, which pays $\max(K - r, 0)$ and insures against falling rates.

c.reason: The payoff is a difference between two rates, not the strike itself. A payoff equal to the strike would not be an option payoff at all, since it would not depend on the realised rate.

d.reason: A payoff equal to the short rate regardless of the strike is an unconditional floating payment, not an option. It has no optionality and therefore no dependence on volatility, which would sever the connection to the LO entirely.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the caplet versus floorlet sibling swap and is the only serious distractor. Bind it with the equity analogue: a caplet is a CALL on a rate, so it pays when the rate goes UP; a floorlet is a PUT on a rate. Note also that a caplet holder is economically a BORROWER hedging against rising funding costs, which is a useful sanity check on the direction.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: In a model where the volatility of the short rate is a deterministic function of time, an analyst reports $\sigma(1) = 1.25\%$ and $\sigma(2) = 1.28\%$, with $t$ measured in years. What do these two values represent?

options.text: The volatility of the short rate over six months is 125 basis points and over one year is 128 basis points.
The volatility of the short rate in one year is 128 basis points per year and in two years is 125 basis points per year.
The volatility of the short rate in one year is 125 basis points per year and in two years is 128 basis points per year.
The time-dependence of the short rate is 125 basis points in one year and 128 basis points in two years.

questions.solution:
Two conventions must both be applied correctly.

The argument is time in years. $\sigma(1)$ is the volatility that applies one year from now, and $\sigma(2)$ is the volatility two years from now. The argument is not an index and not a half-year count.

The units are annualised basis points. One basis point is 0.01%, so:

$\sigma(1) = 1.25\% = 125$ basis points per year

$\sigma(2) = 1.28\% = 128$ basis points per year

Economic reading: the model says the short rate is expected to be slightly MORE volatile two years from now than one year from now, a mild upward slope in the volatility term structure. Note that this is a statement about the volatility applying AT a future date, not about cumulative volatility up to that date.

a.reason: Misreads the argument as half-years. With $t$ in years, $\sigma(1)$ applies at one year, not at six months.

b.reason: Correct on the argument but the two VALUES have been swapped, which reverses the slope of the volatility term structure from rising to falling.

c.reason: Correct argument and correct values, expressed in annualised basis points.

d.reason: 'Time-dependence' is not a quantity and is not measured in basis points. The function is a VOLATILITY that happens to depend on time; the dependence itself is not the thing being measured.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is a value swap that a candidate reading quickly will not catch, because both numbers and both dates are present and only the pairing is wrong. Read the mapping left to right rather than checking that the right numbers appear. Option (d) is the units trap: any answer that assigns basis points to something other than a rate or a volatility is wrong on dimensional grounds alone.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: Model 3 is a special case of the time-dependent volatility specification, written as $dr = \lambda(t)\, dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}\, dw$. Which statement about the behaviour of short-rate volatility in this model is correct?

options.text: Volatility begins at the constant sigma and decays exponentially towards zero.
Volatility begins at the constant lambda and decays exponentially towards zero.
Volatility begins at the constant sigma and grows exponentially without bound.
Volatility begins at zero and rises exponentially towards the constant sigma.

questions.solution:
Isolate the diffusion coefficient of Model 3:

$$\text{volatility at time } t = \sigma \times e^{-\alpha t}$$

Evaluate it at the two ends of the horizon. At $t=0$: $\sigma \times e^0 = \sigma$. As $t$ increases: $e^{-\alpha t}$ falls monotonically towards 0, so volatility falls towards 0.

So volatility starts at $\sigma$ and decays exponentially to zero at rate $\alpha$. The parameter $\alpha$ controls the SPEED of decay: a larger $\alpha$ means volatility dies away faster.

Keep the two parameters in their roles. $\lambda(t)$ is the DRIFT and sits in the $dt$ term; $\sigma$ is the initial VOLATILITY and sits in the $dw$ term. Note also that the decay in Model 3 is a decay in the volatility of the short rate at FUTURE dates, which is a different statement from mean reversion in the rate itself, even though the two produce similar-looking term structures of volatility.

a.reason: At $t=0$ the exponential equals one, so volatility equals $\sigma$; thereafter it decays to zero.

b.reason: Role misassignment. $\lambda$ is the drift parameter and appears in the $dt$ term. It plays no part in setting the level of volatility.

c.reason: Sign error in the exponent. A positive $\alpha$ with a NEGATIVE exponent produces decay. Growth would require $e^{+\alpha t}$.

d.reason: Reverses the direction of travel. The function starts AT $\sigma$ and falls; it does not start at zero and rise towards $\sigma$.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the parameter role swap and is the most commonly selected wrong answer, because lambda and sigma are both Greek constants in the same equation. Locate each parameter by the differential it multiplies: whatever multiplies $dt$ is drift, whatever multiplies $dw$ is volatility. Option (c) is the sign-of-exponent error, which is worth a deliberate check because $e^{-\alpha t}$ and $e^{\alpha t}$ look almost identical under time pressure.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the rate change and the behaviour of its standard deviation
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: An analyst uses Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)\, dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}\, dw$, with $\sigma = 1.50\%$ per year and $\alpha = 0.05$ per year. At $t = 3$ years the drift is $\lambda = 0.30\%$ per year and the interval is one month. Over that month the random variable $dw$ takes the value 0.20. Which is nearest to the change in the short-term rate?
questions.solution:
Step 1. Evaluate the volatility applicable at $t = 3$:

$\sigma(t) = \sigma \times e^{-\alpha t}$

$\sigma(3) = 1.50\% \times e^{-0.05 \times 3} = 1.50\% \times e^{-0.15}$

$\sigma(3) = 1.50\% \times 0.860708 = 1.29106\%$

Volatility has decayed from 1.50% at inception to about 1.29% by year three, a fall of roughly 14%.

Step 2. Compute the drift contribution, scaled by $dt$:

$\lambda \times dt = 0.30\% \times (1/12) = 0.02500\%$

Step 3. Compute the random contribution using the DECAYED volatility:

$\sigma(3) \times dw = 1.29106\% \times 0.20 = 0.25821\%$

Step 4. Add:

$dr = 0.02500\% + 0.25821\% = 0.28321\%$

The rate rises by approximately 28.3 basis points.

On the behaviour of the standard deviation: the annualised standard deviation of the rate change at date $t$ is $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$, which declines monotonically towards zero. Over an interval of length $dt$ the standard deviation is $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}\sqrt{dt}$. Both the decay in $t$ and the square-root scaling in $dt$ apply, and they are independent of one another.

a.reason: 0.2582% is the random term alone. It omits the drift contribution, which is the difference between Model 3 and a driftless specification.

c.reason: $0.3250\% = 0.02500\% + 1.50\% \times 0.20$, which uses the INITIAL volatility sigma and ignores the exponential decay factor entirely. This is the error the question is built to detect, since it reduces Model 3 to Model 2.

d.reason: $0.5582\% = 0.30\% + 0.25821\%$, which adds the ANNUALISED drift without multiplying by $dt$.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the intended kill: it is what you get by reading the process as though sigma were constant, which is precisely the assumption Model 3 exists to relax. Evaluate $e^{-\alpha t}$ FIRST and write the decayed volatility down as a separate line before touching $dw$. Option (d) is the unscaled drift, which recurs across this reading; write 'lambda x dt' rather than 'lambda' as a habit.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Assess the efficacy of time-dependent volatility models
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: Models with time-dependent volatility and models with mean reversion suit different purposes. If the objective is to PRICE a fixed income OPTION, and separately if the objective is to price and hedge fixed income SECURITIES, which models are respectively preferable?

options.text: Time-dependent drift for the option; time-dependent volatility for the securities.
Time-dependent volatility for the option; time-dependent drift for the securities.
Time-dependent volatility for the option; mean reversion for the securities.
Mean reversion for the option; time-dependent volatility for the securities.

questions.solution:
The two model families are good at different things, and the LO asks you to assess rather than merely describe.

| Objective | Preferred model | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Price a fixed income OPTION, especially by interpolating from quoted options | Time-dependent VOLATILITY | $\sigma(t)$ has enough degrees of freedom to match a strip of observed option prices exactly, so unobserved option prices can be interpolated consistently from observed ones |
| Price and HEDGE fixed income securities | MEAN REVERSION | A mean-reverting model produces a realistic term structure of volatility and realistic co-movement across maturities, which is what hedge ratios depend on |

The underlying trade-off is FLEXIBILITY against STRUCTURE. A model with a free function of time can be made to fit almost anything, which is ideal for interpolation and poor for extrapolation or for describing how the curve actually moves. A mean-reverting model imposes economic structure, fits less exactly, and generalises better.

a.reason: Both halves misassigned. Time-dependent DRIFT is calibrated to bond and swap rates, not to option prices; it says nothing about the volatility that option values depend on.

b.reason: The first half is right but the second half substitutes time-dependent drift for mean reversion. Drift calibration matches the level of the curve; it does not deliver the realistic volatility structure that hedging requires.

c.reason: Time-dependent volatility for option pricing and interpolation; mean reversion for pricing and hedging securities.

d.reason: The two answers have been swapped relative to the correct pairing.

trap.explanation: Three distinct concepts are in play and the distractors mix them freely: time-dependent DRIFT (fits the level of the curve), time-dependent VOLATILITY (fits option prices), and MEAN REVERSION (produces realistic dynamics). Fix each to its job before reading the options. The recurring move here is to substitute drift for volatility, since both are 'time-dependent' and the phrase alone does not disambiguate them.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Assess the efficacy of time-dependent volatility models
questions.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
questions.question: Many practitioners object to time-dependent volatility models on the grounds that they imply the market has a specific forecast of short-rate volatility in the DISTANT future. Which modification to the model addresses this objection?

options.text: Assume volatility depends on time in the near term and then settles at a constant thereafter.
Assume the short RATE depends on time in the near term and then settles at a constant.
Assume volatility depends on time in the distant future and settles at an increasing rate.
Assume volatility depends on time in the near term and then decays without limit.

questions.solution:
The objection: a function $\sigma(t)$ specified out to thirty years asserts a precise volatility for every future date. Practitioners find that implausible: it is one thing to say the market has a view on volatility over the next year or two, and quite another to say it has a view on volatility twenty years from now. Under Model 3 in particular, $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$ drives volatility all the way to ZERO in the far future, which asserts that the short rate eventually stops moving. Almost nobody believes that.

The remedy: let volatility be time-dependent over the near horizon, where the market plausibly does have a view and where option prices provide information, and then hold it CONSTANT beyond some date:

$\sigma(t) = $ a time-dependent function for $t \le T^*$, then $\sigma(t) = $ constant for $t > T^*$

This preserves the flexibility needed to fit near-dated option prices while removing the indefensible claim about the distant future, and it stops volatility from decaying to zero.

Assessment: the fix is a compromise, not a solution. It concedes that the model's flexibility is an artefact of calibration rather than a description of reality, which is the general reason mean-reverting models are preferred where structure matters.

a.reason: Time-dependence retained where information exists, constant volatility imposed beyond it.

b.reason: Applies the fix to the wrong quantity. The objection concerns the path of VOLATILITY, not the path of the rate. Fixing the rate at a constant would remove the stochastic behaviour the model exists to represent.

c.reason: Inverts the fix. The objection is precisely that the model asserts too much about the DISTANT future, so leaving time-dependence there and, worse, letting it increase, aggravates the problem rather than curing it.

d.reason: Unlimited decay is the original problem, not the remedy. Model 3 already drives volatility to zero, which is exactly what practitioners object to.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the direction reversal and is tempting to anyone who has registered the words 'distant future' as the topic without registering that they name the PROBLEM. Read the objection first and state what needs to be removed, then look for the option that removes it. Option (b) is the quantity swap between rate and volatility, which recurs throughout this reading.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: A quanto option allows a domestic investor to convert an option payoff denominated in a foreign currency back into the domestic currency at a FIXED exchange rate, protecting the investor against currency risk. From a risk management standpoint, which two quantities does the institution SELLING the quanto option not know in advance?

options.text: The amount of foreign currency that will need to be converted, and the exchange rate at maturity at which the conversion would otherwise have taken place.
The amount of domestic currency that will need to be converted, and the exchange rate at maturity at which the conversion would otherwise have taken place.
Which foreign currency is correlated with the domestic currency, and the size of that correlation.
The strike price of the option, and the volatility of the underlying at maturity.

questions.solution:
The seller of a quanto option faces two independent uncertainties that interact.

Unknown 1: how much foreign currency will be needed. The payoff is an option payoff on a foreign asset, so its size depends on where that asset finishes. The seller does not know the notional amount of foreign currency that will have to be delivered.

Unknown 2: the exchange rate at maturity. The investor is guaranteed a FIXED conversion rate. The seller must actually source the currency at the PREVAILING rate and absorb the difference.

Neither uncertainty is unusual on its own. What makes the quanto a correlation product is that the two interact. The seller's loss is largest when a big payoff coincides with an adverse exchange rate, and how often that happens is governed by the CORRELATION between the underlying asset and the exchange rate. That correlation is itself unobservable and unstable, which is the risk management point.

Note the asymmetry in the currency direction. The payoff arises in FOREIGN currency and is delivered in DOMESTIC currency, so it is the foreign amount that is unknown and must be converted.

a.reason: The unknown quantity is the foreign currency amount, and the unknown price is the exchange rate at maturity.

b.reason: Currency direction reversed. The option pays off in the FOREIGN currency; the domestic amount is what the investor receives after conversion at the fixed rate, and from the investor's perspective it is determined by the fixed rate.

c.reason: The seller knows perfectly well which currency pair is involved, since it is written into the contract. What is unknown is the LEVEL of the correlation and its stability, not its identity.

d.reason: The strike is contractually fixed and known at inception. Volatility of the underlying is an input the seller must estimate, but it is not one of the two quanto-specific unknowns, and it applies equally to an ordinary option.

trap.explanation: Option (b) is the currency-direction flip and is the only serious distractor. Fix the direction by asking where the payoff ARISES: a quanto is written on a foreign asset, so the raw payoff is foreign and the conversion runs foreign to domestic. Option (d) is the ordinary-option trap: it names two real inputs, neither of which is specific to a quanto, so it fails to answer the question actually asked.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: A domestic investor buys a quanto CALL on a foreign equity index, with the payoff converted into domestic currency at a fixed exchange rate. Let $\rho$ be the correlation between the foreign equity index and the exchange rate expressed as units of domestic currency per unit of foreign currency. Holding all else equal, what is the effect of an increase in $\rho$ on the value of the quanto call?

options.text: The value of the quanto call rises.
The effect cannot be signed without knowing the volatility of the exchange rate.
The value of the quanto call is unaffected, because the conversion rate is fixed.
The value of the quanto call falls.

questions.solution:
Because the payoff is converted at a FIXED rate, the seller cannot hedge the currency exposure with a simple forward: the amount to be converted is itself uncertain. Pricing the contract in the domestic risk-neutral measure requires adjusting the drift of the foreign asset by a covariance term. The resulting quanto drift is:

$$\mu_{quanto} = r_{foreign} - q - \rho\, \sigma(S)\, \sigma(E)$$

where $\sigma(S)$ is the volatility of the foreign asset, $\sigma(E)$ is the volatility of the exchange rate, and $\rho$ is the correlation between them.

Sign the effect directly from the formula. The correlation term enters with a MINUS sign, so a higher $\rho$ lowers the effective drift of the foreign asset under the pricing measure. A lower drift reduces the value of a CALL and raises the value of a PUT.

$\rho$ increases $\Rightarrow \mu_{quanto}$ falls $\Rightarrow$ quanto CALL falls, quanto PUT rises.

Intuition for the sign: high positive correlation means the foreign asset tends to rise exactly when the foreign currency is strong. The seller has promised a fixed conversion rate, so all of that currency upside accrues to the seller rather than the buyer. The buyer is giving something up, so the buyer pays less.

The SIZE of the effect does depend on both volatilities, since they multiply $\rho$. The DIRECTION does not, because volatilities are non-negative.

a.reason: The correlation term is subtracted from the drift, so higher correlation reduces rather than increases the value of a call.

b.reason: The two volatilities scale the magnitude of the adjustment but cannot change its sign, since both are non-negative. The direction is determined by the sign of $\rho$ alone.

c.reason: Fixing the conversion rate is what CREATES the correlation exposure rather than removing it. If the payoff were converted at the prevailing spot rate there would be no quanto adjustment and no correlation term at all.

d.reason: The correlation enters the quanto drift with a negative sign, depressing the call.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the strongest distractor and it inverts the economics: the fixed rate is the source of the exposure, not a hedge against it. Option (b) is the false-humility trap, made attractive because it correctly senses that volatilities are involved. Whenever a parameter multiplies a non-negative quantity, the sign of the effect follows the parameter alone.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: A structuring desk prices two products on the same pair of underlying assets: an EXCHANGE option, which pays $\max(S_1 - S_2, 0)$, and a BASKET call on the equally weighted average of the two assets. What is the effect of an increase in the correlation between the two assets on the value of each?

options.text: Both values rise, because higher correlation raises the volatility of any multi-asset payoff.
Both values fall, because higher correlation reduces diversification within the structure.
The exchange option falls in value and the basket call rises.
The exchange option rises in value and the basket call falls.

questions.solution:
Both products are options on a linear combination of the two assets, so in each case the value rises with the volatility of that combination. The two combinations respond to correlation in opposite ways.

Exchange option: the volatility of a DIFFERENCE.

$$\text{Var}(S_1 - S_2) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$$

The correlation term is SUBTRACTED. Higher correlation means the two assets move together, so their difference moves less, so the option is worth less. At $\rho = 1$ with equal volatilities the spread is deterministic and the option is nearly worthless.

Basket option: the volatility of a SUM.

$$\text{Var}(w_1 S_1 + w_2 S_2) = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2 w_1 w_2 \rho \sigma_1 \sigma_2$$

The correlation term is ADDED. Higher correlation means less diversification within the basket, a more volatile basket, and a more valuable option. At $\rho = 1$ the basket is as volatile as its components and the diversification benefit vanishes entirely.

| Product | Depends on the volatility of | Effect of higher rho |
|---|---|---|
| Exchange option, spread option | a DIFFERENCE | value FALLS |
| Basket option, index option | a SUM | value RISES |
| Worst-of call | the minimum of the assets | value RISES (less dispersion) |
| Best-of call | the maximum of the assets | value FALLS (less dispersion) |

a.reason: Higher correlation does not raise the volatility of every multi-asset payoff. It raises the volatility of a SUM and lowers the volatility of a DIFFERENCE. Applying one rule to both is the error the question is built to detect.

b.reason: Also applies a single rule to both, in the other direction. Reduced diversification is exactly why the BASKET becomes more valuable; it is not a reason for both to fall.

c.reason: The difference becomes less volatile and the sum more volatile, so the exchange option falls and the basket call rises.

d.reason: The two effects have been swapped. The exchange option depends on the volatility of a difference, which falls with correlation.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (b) both apply a single blanket rule and between them will collect most of the wrong answers, because 'correlation reduces diversification' is a slogan that gets applied indiscriminately. The discriminating question is always the same: does the payoff depend on a SUM or on a DIFFERENCE? Write the variance expression and read the sign in front of the $2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ term.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the structure, uses and payoffs of a correlation swap
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: A volatility desk is considering entering a correlation swap. Which of the following best describes the structure and typical use of the instrument?

options.text: An exchange-traded contract in which the buyer receives a payoff only if realised correlation exceeds the fixed rate, making it an option on correlation.
A contract whose payoff depends on the correlation between an equity index and its own implied volatility, used principally to hedge quanto exposures.
An over-the-counter contract in which both parties exchange the realised variances of the individual assets in a basket, used to hedge dispersion risk.

An over-the-counter contract in which the buyer of correlation pays a fixed correlation rate and receives the realised average pairwise correlation of a basket on a notional, used to take a directional view on correlation or to hedge an existing short-correlation exposure.

questions.solution:
Structure. A correlation swap is an over-the-counter contract on a specified basket of assets. One party, the buyer of correlation, pays a FIXED correlation rate agreed at inception. At maturity the parties settle on:

$$\text{payoff to the buyer} = \text{Notional} \times [\rho_{realised} - \rho_{fixed}]$$

The payoff is LINEAR and SYMMETRIC. If realised correlation falls below the fixed rate the buyer pays. That is what makes it a swap rather than an option.

Uses. Two principal ones:

| Use | Who | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Directional view on correlation | Volatility and macro desks | Correlation rises sharply in crises, so buying correlation is a way of being long systemic stress |
| Hedging an existing short-correlation position | Structured products desks, dispersion traders | Selling index options while buying single-name options leaves a desk short correlation; a correlation swap hedges that exposure directly rather than through a basket of options |

The second use is the important one commercially. A desk that has sold index volatility and bought single-name volatility is implicitly short correlation, and its losses arrive precisely when correlations spike. A correlation swap isolates and offsets that exposure without requiring the desk to unwind a large book of options.

a.reason: Two defects. Correlation swaps trade over the counter, not on an exchange; and the payoff is symmetric, so the buyer can lose. A one-sided payoff would make the instrument an option, which would require an upfront premium rather than a fixed rate.

b.reason: The correlation between an index and its own implied volatility is a different quantity, and quanto exposures involve the correlation between an asset and an EXCHANGE RATE. Neither is what a correlation swap references.

c.reason: This describes the components of a DISPERSION trade, which exchanges index variance against single-name variance. A dispersion trade gives correlated exposure to correlation but is not a correlation swap, and its payoff depends on variances rather than on a correlation directly.

d.reason: OTC, symmetric linear payoff on realised average pairwise correlation, used for directional views and for hedging short-correlation books.

trap.explanation: Option (c) is the strongest distractor because a dispersion trade is the closest economic substitute for a correlation swap and is often discussed alongside it. The distinction is what the contract REFERENCES: a correlation swap settles on a correlation directly, while a dispersion trade settles on variances and delivers correlation exposure only as a by-product. Option (a) is the swap-versus-option confusion, and the tell is that a genuine swap has no premium and can pay in either direction.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Estimate the impact of correlation on the VaR capital charge
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: An analyst observes that the correlation between two assets held long in a portfolio is NEGATIVE. What does this imply?

options.text: When one asset falls in value the other tends to fall as well, which reduces overall portfolio risk.
When one asset rises in value the other tends to rise as well, which reduces overall portfolio risk.
When one asset falls in value the other tends to rise, which increases overall portfolio risk.
When one asset falls in value the other tends to rise, which reduces overall portfolio risk.

questions.solution:
Negative correlation means the two assets tend to move in OPPOSITE directions. For a portfolio held long in both, that is a risk-reducing property.

$$\text{Var(portfolio)} = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2 w_1 w_2 \rho \sigma_1 \sigma_2$$

With both weights positive, the cross term carries the sign of $\rho$. A negative $\rho$ makes the cross term negative and pulls portfolio variance BELOW the sum of the individual contributions. Losses on one holding are partly offset by gains on the other, which is diversification in its purest form.

Two boundary cases are worth carrying:

| Correlation | Cross term | Portfolio risk |
|---|---|---|
| $\rho = +1$ | maximally positive | No diversification. Portfolio volatility is the weighted sum of the individual volatilities. |
| $\rho = 0$ | zero | Partial diversification. Volatilities add in quadrature. |
| $\rho = -1$ | maximally negative | Maximum diversification. A hedge ratio exists that drives portfolio variance to zero. |

The caveat that makes correlation a RISK rather than merely a parameter: correlations are not stable. Negative correlations observed in calm markets have a documented tendency to move towards positive in a crisis, which removes the diversification exactly when it is most needed.

a.reason: Describes POSITIVE correlation in its first clause, since assets falling together move in the same direction. The second clause then attaches the risk-reduction conclusion that belongs to negative correlation, so the option is internally inconsistent.

b.reason: Describes positive correlation. Assets rising together move in the same direction, which reduces rather than provides diversification.

c.reason: The first clause correctly describes negative correlation but the conclusion is reversed. Offsetting movements reduce the variance of the combination; they do not increase it.

d.reason: Opposite movement, and risk reduction for a long-long portfolio.

trap.explanation: Options (a) and (c) are each half right, which is the standard construction: one gets the DIRECTION of the co-movement right and the CONSEQUENCE wrong, the other the reverse. Check both clauses of every option independently. Note also that the risk-reduction conclusion depends on both positions being LONG; for a long-short portfolio the signs invert, which is the scope condition tested elsewhere in this reading.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Estimate the impact of correlation on the VaR capital charge
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: For a portfolio holding LONG positions in two assets, which value of the correlation between the assets yields the HIGHEST portfolio value at risk?
questions.solution:
Portfolio variance for two long positions is:

$$\text{Var}(p) = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2 w_1 w_2 \rho \sigma_1 \sigma_2$$

Everything except $\rho$ is fixed by the stem. With $w_1$, $w_2$, $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ all positive, the coefficient on $\rho$ is strictly positive, so portfolio variance is strictly INCREASING in $\rho$. Portfolio VaR under the variance-covariance approach is a positive multiple of the portfolio standard deviation, so VaR inherits the same monotonicity.

$$\text{VaR}(p) = z \times \sqrt{\text{Var}(p)} \times \text{Portfolio value}$$

The maximum over the four offered values therefore occurs at the largest $\rho$, which is 1. At $\rho = 1$ the diversification benefit vanishes completely and portfolio VaR collapses to the simple SUM of the individual VaRs:

at $\rho = 1$: $\text{VaR}(p) = \text{VaR}(1) + \text{VaR}(2)$

This is the useful shortcut. Rather than computing four portfolio variances, recognise that the answer is a monotonicity result and read off the extreme value. The undiversified sum is always the upper bound on portfolio VaR for a long-only portfolio, which is exactly why subadditivity is expected to hold here.

a.reason: A correlation of -0.5 produces the LOWEST VaR of the four, since the cross term is most strongly negative among the values offered.

b.reason: Zero correlation gives partial diversification: the cross term vanishes and volatilities combine in quadrature. VaR is lower than at any positive correlation.

c.reason: Correlation of 0.5 gives a higher VaR than 0 or -0.5 but lower than 1. It is the trap for a candidate who reasons that 'moderate' correlation is somehow the realistic worst case.

d.reason: Perfect positive correlation removes all diversification and maximises portfolio VaR.

trap.explanation: This is a shortcut item: no computation is required once VaR is seen to be monotone in rho. A candidate who computes four portfolio standard deviations reaches the same answer but loses time doing so, a timing failure even though the answer is right. The content trap is the scope condition LONG: for a portfolio that is long one asset and SHORT the other, the cross term reverses sign and VaR is MAXIMISED at rho = -1.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Estimate the impact of correlation on the VaR capital charge
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: A portfolio of USD 10 million is invested in two assets X and Y in the ratio 6:4. The volatilities of the two assets are 5% and 10% respectively. Using the variance-covariance approach with a normal deviate of 2.33, what is the portfolio VaR at the 99% confidence level if the assets are (i) perfectly correlated and (ii) uncorrelated?

options.text: Perfectly correlated USD 1.16m; uncorrelated USD 1.63m
Perfectly correlated USD 1.15m; uncorrelated USD 0.82m
Perfectly correlated USD 1.86m; uncorrelated USD 1.47m
Perfectly correlated USD 1.63m; uncorrelated USD 1.16m

questions.solution:
Step 1. Compute the individual VaRs. The 6:4 ratio gives USD 6 million in X and USD 4 million in Y.

$\text{VaR}(X) = 6.0 \times 0.05 \times 2.33 = \text{USD } 0.699$ million, approximately 0.70

$\text{VaR}(Y) = 4.0 \times 0.10 \times 2.33 = \text{USD } 0.932$ million, approximately 0.93

Step 2. Perfectly correlated case. With $\rho = 1$ there is no diversification and the individual VaRs simply add.

$\text{VaR}(p) = \text{VaR}(X) + \text{VaR}(Y) = 0.70 + 0.93 = \text{USD } 1.63$ million

Step 3. Uncorrelated case. With $\rho = 0$ the cross term vanishes and the VaRs combine in quadrature.

$\text{VaR}(p) = \sqrt{0.70^2 + 0.93^2} = \sqrt{0.49 + 0.8649} = \sqrt{1.3549} = \text{USD } 1.16$ million

The diversification benefit is $1.63 - 1.16 = \text{USD } 0.47$ million, or about 29% of the undiversified figure. Note that the perfectly correlated case is always the LARGER of the two, which is the numerical expression of the monotonicity result above and a free sanity check on the answer.

a.reason: The two figures are correct but assigned to the wrong cases. Perfect correlation must give the HIGHER number, since it removes diversification.

b.reason: USD 1.15m and 0.82m use the 95% normal deviate of 1.645 rather than the 2.33 specified in the stem.

c.reason: USD 1.86m and 1.47m result from inverting the 6:4 split and placing USD 4 million in X and USD 6 million in Y. The more volatile asset then carries the larger weight, inflating both figures.

d.reason: USD 1.63 million perfectly correlated, USD 1.16 million uncorrelated.

trap.explanation: Option (a) is the intended kill and requires no arithmetic error at all: the candidate does both calculations correctly and then assigns them to the wrong labels. Before selecting, ask which case should be LARGER and check that your answer respects it. Perfect correlation is always the upper bound for a long-only portfolio.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Estimate the impact of correlation on the VaR capital charge
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: A portfolio of USD 10 million consists of two assets, A and B, with values of USD 3 million and USD 7 million respectively. The daily standard deviations are 3% for A and 5% for B, and the correlation between them is 0.4. Using the variance-covariance approach with a normal deviate of 2.33, what is the one-day 99% portfolio VaR?

options.text: USD 0.65 million
USD 0.84 million
USD 0.92 million
USD 1.02 million

questions.solution:
Step 1. Compute portfolio variance from the weights, volatilities and correlation. The weights are 0.3 and 0.7.

$$\text{Var}(p) = w_A^2\sigma_A^2 + w_B^2\sigma_B^2 + 2 w_A w_B \rho \sigma_A \sigma_B$$

term 1 $= 0.30^2 \times 0.03^2 = 0.09 \times 0.0009 = 0.0000810$

term 2 $= 0.70^2 \times 0.05^2 = 0.49 \times 0.0025 = 0.0012250$

term 3 $= 2 \times 0.30 \times 0.70 \times 0.40 \times 0.03 \times 0.05 = 0.0002520$

$\text{Var}(p) = 0.0000810 + 0.0012250 + 0.0002520 = 0.0015580$

Step 2. Take the square root to obtain the portfolio standard deviation.

$\sigma(p) = \sqrt{0.0015580} = 0.039472$, that is 3.9472% per day

Step 3. Scale to a VaR.

$\text{VaR} = 10.0 \times 0.039472 \times 2.33 = \text{USD } 0.9197$ million, approximately 0.92

Sanity check against the boundary cases: the individual VaRs are $3.0 \times 0.03 \times 2.33 = 0.2097$ and $7.0 \times 0.05 \times 2.33 = 0.8155$. Zero correlation would give $\sqrt{0.2097^2 + 0.8155^2} = 0.84$, and perfect correlation would give $0.2097 + 0.8155 = 1.02$. The answer of 0.92 sits between them, exactly as a correlation of 0.4 requires.

a.reason: USD 0.65 million applies the 95% normal deviate of 1.645 rather than the 2.33 specified.

b.reason: USD 0.84 million is the ZERO-correlation result. It omits the cross term entirely, which is the same as assuming the assets are independent and discards the information the question supplies.

c.reason: USD 0.92 million, computed above.

d.reason: USD 1.02 million is the PERFECT-correlation result, the simple sum of the individual VaRs. It over-applies the correlation by treating rho = 0.4 as rho = 1.

trap.explanation: The three wrong answers are deliberately the two boundary cases plus a confidence-level slip, so the option set itself teaches the ordering: 0.84 at rho = 0, then 0.92 at rho = 0.4, then 1.02 at rho = 1. If your answer falls outside that band you have made an error before you check anything else. The commonest slip inside the correct path is dropping the factor of 2 in the cross term.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: Which statement best characterises the relationship between systemic risk and correlation risk?

options.text: They are largely independent of one another.
They are only weakly related, since systemic risk concerns solvency while correlation risk concerns market prices.
They are highly dependent, because a systemic event causes correlations across asset classes to rise sharply and simultaneously.
They are inversely related, because diversification across institutions reduces systemic risk.

questions.solution:
Systemic risk is the risk of disruption to the financial system as a whole rather than to a single institution or asset. Correlation risk is the risk of loss arising from changes in the correlations between financial quantities. The two are tightly coupled, and the coupling runs in both directions.

| Direction | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Systemic event causes correlation change | In a crisis investors sell whatever is liquid rather than whatever is overvalued. Assets with no fundamental link fall together, so correlations across asset classes converge towards one. |
| Correlation change causes systemic loss | Portfolios, hedges and capital models are calibrated to normal-period correlations. When correlations spike, diversification disappears exactly when it is needed, hedges fail together, and losses arrive simultaneously across institutions. |

The practical consequence is that measured risk is systematically understated before a crisis. A portfolio whose VaR is computed from calm-period correlations is not merely wrong in a crisis, it is wrong in the direction that matters, because the diversification credit embedded in the calculation evaporates precisely when losses occur.

a.reason: The empirical record contradicts independence directly. Correlations across almost all risky asset classes rose towards one during the 2007 to 2009 crisis.

b.reason: The distinction drawn is artificial. Systemic events transmit through market prices, and solvency is assessed on marked positions, so the two channels are the same channel.

c.reason: Highly dependent, with correlations rising sharply and simultaneously in a systemic event.

d.reason: Confuses two different applications of diversification. Diversification WITHIN a portfolio reduces that portfolio's risk; homogeneity ACROSS institutions, where everyone holds similar diversified portfolios, increases systemic risk rather than reducing it. The claimed inverse relationship also contradicts the observed behaviour of correlations in a crisis.

trap.explanation: Option (d) is the most instructive distractor because it deploys a genuinely correct principle, diversification reduces risk, at the wrong level of aggregation. Diversification is protective for one portfolio and can be corrosive for the system, since it drives every institution towards the same holdings and therefore towards simultaneous losses. Ask always WHOSE risk is being reduced. Option (b) is the false-dichotomy trap between market and credit channels, which in a systemic event are not separable.

questions.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: Concentration risk is the risk of financial loss arising from a concentrated exposure to a group of counterparties, and it can be quantified with a concentration ratio. What is the correct rule of thumb for a creditor?

options.text: The LOWER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the LOWER the overall portfolio default risk.
The HIGHER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the LOWER the overall portfolio default risk.
The LOWER the concentration ratio, the LOWER the diversification, and the HIGHER the overall portfolio default risk.
The HIGHER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the HIGHER the overall portfolio default risk.

questions.solution:
For a creditor with $n$ loans of equal size to distinct entities, the concentration ratio is:

$$\text{concentration ratio} = 1/n$$

| Number of equal-sized loans | Concentration ratio | Diversification |
|---|---|---|
| 1 borrower | 1.00 | None. All exposure to a single name. |
| 3 borrowers | 0.333 | Modest |
| 100 borrowers | 0.01 | High |

The direction is fixed by the reciprocal. More borrowers means a LOWER ratio and MORE diversification, so a lower ratio corresponds to lower portfolio default risk. The chain runs: more borrowers $\rightarrow$ lower concentration ratio $\rightarrow$ higher diversification $\rightarrow$ lower portfolio default risk.

A worked illustration: a bank lends 10,000 to a single borrower with a 10% default probability. Its concentration ratio is 1 and its expected loss is $10{,}000 \times 0.10 = 1{,}000$. If instead it lends the same 10,000 across three borrowers each with a 10% default probability, the concentration ratio falls to $1/3$. Expected loss is unchanged at 1,000, because expectation is linear, but the DISPERSION of loss falls sharply and the probability of losing the entire 10,000 collapses from 10% to 0.1% under independence. Concentration risk is a statement about the tail, not about the mean.

The scope condition that makes this work: the benefit requires default correlation below one. If all borrowers default together, spreading the loan across three names changes nothing.

a.reason: Lower ratio, higher diversification, lower risk. All three clauses aligned.

b.reason: The first clause is reversed. A HIGHER ratio means FEWER effective borrowers and therefore LESS diversification.

c.reason: The first clause is right but the second and third are reversed. A lower ratio gives MORE diversification and LOWER risk.

d.reason: Internally inconsistent as well as wrong: it claims higher diversification and higher risk simultaneously, which contradicts the definition of diversification.

trap.explanation: All four options are built from the same three clauses with signs permuted, so the item is won by checking each clause independently rather than by pattern-matching to a familiar-looking sentence. Anchor on the arithmetic rather than the words: the ratio is 1/n, so more names means a SMALLER number. Once that is fixed, the remaining two clauses follow. Option (d) can be eliminated on internal inconsistency alone without any knowledge of the reading.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
questions.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
questions.question: A lending institution wants to reduce the default correlation within its loan portfolio. Which of the following is the most appropriate policy?

options.text: Intersector default correlations are typically HIGHER than intrasector correlations, so the lender should specialise in a single sector.
Intrasector default correlations are typically HIGHER than intersector correlations, so the lender should build a sector-diversified loan portfolio.
Intrasector default correlations are typically LOWER than intersector correlations, so the lender should specialise in a single sector.
Default correlations are approximately equal within and across sectors, so the composition of the portfolio by sector is not a useful lever.

questions.solution:
Get the two terms straight before anything else:

| Term | Meaning | Typical level |
|---|---|---|
| INTRAsector | Between borrowers WITHIN the same sector | HIGHER |
| INTERsector | Between borrowers in DIFFERENT sectors | LOWER |

Firms in the same sector share customers, input costs, regulation and demand conditions, so a shock to the sector hits them together. Firms in unrelated sectors share only economy-wide factors, so their defaults are less tightly linked.

The policy follows directly. Because intrasector correlation is the higher of the two, a lender concentrated in one sector holds a portfolio of highly correlated exposures and gets little tail protection from the number of loans.
