A deep in-the-money call is struck low and has a delta near 1.0; a deep out-of-the-money call is struck high and has a delta near 0.0. Since the axis is ordered by increasing strike, the sequence of call deltas must fall monotonically from left to right.

**Fact 2: one-to-one mapping.** Delta is a strictly monotone function of strike, so no delta value can appear twice on the curve. Any sequence that falls and then rises, or rises and then falls, is impossible for a single instrument type.

The market shorthand labels these five points as 10, 25, 50, 25, 10 – meaning the 10-delta put, the 25-delta put, at the money, the 25-delta call, and the 10-delta call. That labelling looks symmetric only because it switches instrument at the middle point. Expressed consistently:

- as call deltas: $[0.90,\ 0.75,\ 0.50,\ 0.25,\ 0.10]$
- as put deltas: $[-0.10,\ -0.25,\ -0.50,\ -0.75,\ -0.90]$

Delta is used as an axis because it embeds time to maturity, since delta depends on $T$ as well as on moneyness, and it extends the smile to instruments other than European and American calls and puts. Under this convention an at-the-money option is defined as a 0.50-delta call or a $-0.50$-delta put, referred to as 50-delta options.

a.reason: Monotonically decreasing, matching increasing strike, and expressed as actual rather than shorthand deltas.

b.reason: Monotonic but in the wrong direction. This ordering would require strike to decrease from left to right, contradicting the stem.

c.reason: This is the market shorthand read literally as a list of actual call deltas. Delta cannot take the same value at two different strikes, so the sequence is impossible.

d.reason: Two defects: it has the same impossible non-monotonicity as a literal reading of the shorthand, and the sign is wrong. A long European put has a strictly negative delta, bounded between $-1.0$ and 0, so a list of positive put deltas cannot exist.

trap.explanation: The stem explicitly warns against reading the market shorthand literally, because doing so produces a sequence that repeats a delta value at two different strikes, which is impossible for a monotone function. A related distractor compounds that same non-monotonicity with a sign error, since put deltas are strictly negative; checking the sign is the fastest available elimination.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe alternative ways of characterizing the volatility smile
questions.reading: Hull, Ch. 20: Volatility Smiles
questions.question:
The implied distribution of a certain asset class exhibits, relative to the lognormal distribution, a LIGHTER left tail and a HEAVIER right tail. A trader defines the risk reversal as the difference in implied volatility, computed under BSM, between a 0.25 delta call and a $-0.25$ delta put:

$$RR = \sigma_{imp}[0.25\text{ delta call}] - \sigma_{imp}[-0.25\text{ delta put}]$$

Which of the following is most likely true of the risk reversal?

options.text: The risk reversal is negative.
The risk reversal is zero.
The risk reversal is positive.
The risk reversal is approximately equal to the implied volatility of the 0.50 delta call, that is, the at-the-money call.

questions.solution:
This question covers the risk reversal as a scalar summary of the direction of skew, and its sign under a reverse (upward-sloping) skew.

**Step 1. Translate tails into a slope.** A lighter left tail means low-strike options are relatively cheap, so implied volatility is low at low strikes. A heavier right tail means high-strike options are relatively expensive, so implied volatility is high at high strikes. Implied volatility is therefore an increasing function of strike: an upward-sloping, or reverse, or forward skew – the opposite of the usual equity pattern.

**Step 2. Locate the two legs.** A 0.25 delta call has a delta well below 0.50, so it is out of the money and struck high. A $-0.25$ delta put has a delta between $-0.50$ and 0, so it is also out of the money and struck low. Both legs are out-of-the-money options, one on each wing, which is exactly what makes the risk reversal a measure of skew rather than of level.

**Step 3. Sign it.** The call leg sits on the high-strike side, where implied volatility is high. The put leg sits on the low-strike side, where implied volatility is low. Therefore:

$$RR = (\text{high implied volatility}) - (\text{low implied volatility}) > 0$$

The risk reversal is positive. As a sanity check on the general rule: a negative risk reversal is the signature of the standard equity skew, where out-of-the-money puts carry higher implied volatility than out-of-the-money calls.

a.reason: A negative risk reversal corresponds to the usual equity skew, in which out-of-the-money puts carry higher implied volatility than out-of-the-money calls – the default answer for anyone who reflexively assumes an equity-shaped curve.

b.reason: A zero risk reversal corresponds to a symmetric curve, either perfectly flat or a symmetric smile. The stem describes an explicitly asymmetric distribution.

c.reason: Positive, because the out-of-the-money call sits where implied volatility is high and the out-of-the-money put sits where it is low.

d.reason: A category error. A risk reversal is a difference of two implied volatilities and therefore measures skew. At-the-money implied volatility measures level. Numerically the two are not comparable: a risk reversal is typically a few volatility points while the at-the-money level runs to tens of points.

trap.explanation: The main trap targets anyone who has over-drilled the standard equity skew and now treats a negative risk reversal as the default, when the stem explicitly describes the reverse case. The discipline is to read the tail description first and convert it into a slope before touching the deltas; a further distractor confuses a difference (skew) with a level (at-the-money volatility), which can be eliminated on dimensional grounds alone.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the CALCULATION of an option's Greek letter risk measures
questions.reading: Hull, Ch. 20: Volatility Smiles
questions.question: A newly hired analyst asserts that because BSM vega is always positive and peaks for at-the-money options, the implied volatility smile must be hump-shaped with a peak at the money. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: The analyst is correct; the vega profile and the implied volatility smile are two views of the same underlying function.
If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, then Greek vega is zero.
Vega is the first derivative of the implied volatility smile; that is, it plots the slopes of lines tangent to the implied volatility plot.

Under BSM, vega is always positive and highest for an at-the-money option, but these properties neither predict nor constrain the shape of the corresponding implied volatility smile, which is free to be a skew, a smirk, a frown, or any other shape.

questions.solution:
This question tests that vega is a model-based partial derivative computed at a point, while the smile is a market-determined artefact; they are different objects with different axes.

| | Vega | Implied volatility smile |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | First partial derivative of the BSM option value with respect to the volatility input | The set of volatility inputs that force the BSM price to equal each observed market price |
| Determined by | The model alone | Market prices: supply, demand, and beliefs about the true distribution |
| Axes | Option value sensitivity, plotted against asset price or strike, with volatility held fixed | Implied volatility, plotted against strike, with volatility solved for |

Vega is positive because more volatility is always worth more to an option holder. That positivity is what makes the price-to-volatility mapping monotone and therefore invertible, which is what allows the smile to be constructed at all. But knowing that vega is positive and hump-shaped tells you nothing about where market prices will sit relative to a single-volatility model, and therefore nothing about the shape of the smile.

The BSM model assumes the underlying follows a lognormal distribution with constant volatility. Vega measures the rate of change of the option price given a change in that constant. Shifts in supply and demand can produce any smile shape without changing vega's qualitative profile at all.

a.reason: Different objects with different axes. The vega hump is model output; the smile is constructed from market input. Neither implies the other.

b.reason: This is the sharpest distractor. A flat smile means a single implied volatility prices every strike correctly, which is the BSM world working exactly as designed. Vega remains strictly positive in that world. The error is confusing 'the smile has zero slope' with 'vega is zero', which conflates the derivative of implied volatility with respect to strike with the derivative of price with respect to volatility.

c.reason: Both arguments are swapped. Vega is the derivative of option price with respect to volatility. The slope of the smile is the derivative of implied volatility with respect to strike.

d.reason: Vega's properties are real but carry no implication for the shape of the smile.

trap.explanation: The decisive distractor exploits the natural-sounding chain 'flat suggests zero derivative suggests zero vega', requiring the solver to name both variables of any derivative before agreeing with a claim about it: vega is the derivative of price with respect to volatility, while smile slope is the derivative of implied volatility with respect to strike. Other distractors either equate the two objects outright or swap which variable belongs to which derivative.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the CALCULATION of an option's Greek letter risk measures
questions.reading: Hull, Ch. 20: Volatility Smiles
questions.question: A one-year at-the-money call struck at USD 100.00 trades at USD 13.28, from which an analyst infers an implied volatility of 30.0% per annum. Under BSM the call's delta, $N(d_1)$, is 0.60, so the put with the same strike and maturity carries a BSM delta of $N(d_1) - 1.0 = 0.60 - 1.0 = -0.40$. However, the equity option exhibits a steep implied volatility skew which implies, relative to the lognormal distribution, a heavy left tail and a light right tail: implied volatility is a DECREASING function of $K/S(0)$. Which of the following describes the relationship between the TRUE deltas and the BSM deltas?

options.text: True call delta is HIGHER than 0.60, and true put delta is HIGHER than $-0.40$.
True call delta is LOWER than 0.60, and true put delta is LOWER than $-0.40$.
True call delta equals 0.60, and true put delta equals $-0.40$.
The relationship cannot be determined, because delta is only a first-order approximation.

questions.solution:
This question shows how the existence of a smile adds a second term to delta, with the sign of that term following directly from the slope of the skew, and put-call parity then fixing the put delta.

BSM delta holds volatility constant as the asset price moves. In reality, when the asset price moves the option's implied volatility moves too, because the option's position on the smile changes. Extend delta by the chain rule:

$$\text{true delta} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial S} + \frac{\partial c}{\partial \sigma_{imp}} \times \frac{\partial \sigma_{imp}}{\partial S}$$

The first term is the BSM delta, 0.60. The second term is vega multiplied by the sensitivity of implied volatility to the asset price. Sign each factor separately.

$$\text{vega} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial \sigma_{imp}} > 0 \quad \text{(always, for any option)}$$

For the skew factor: implied volatility is a decreasing function of $K/S(0)$. The strike $K$ is fixed for a given option, so when $S$ rises, $K/S(0)$ falls, and therefore implied volatility rises:

$$\frac{\partial \sigma_{imp}}{\partial S} > 0 \quad \text{(the standard equity-option result)}$$

The product of two positive quantities is positive, so the second term adds to the BSM delta:

$$\text{true call delta} > 0.60$$

For the put, put-call parity fixes the relationship between the deltas exactly:

$$p = c - S + Ke^{-rT} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial p}{\partial S} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial S} - 1$$
$$\text{true put delta} = \text{true call delta} - 1 > 0.60 - 1 = -0.40$$

So the true put delta is also higher than $-0.40$, meaning closer to zero, that is, less negative. Both deltas shift by exactly the same amount.

a.reason: Both terms are positive for the call, and parity carries the same shift to the put.

b.reason: This would follow from a skew in which implied volatility increases in $K/S(0)$, that is, the reverse-skew case, not the equity case described in the stem.

c.reason: This is the answer obtained by ignoring the second term entirely, that is, by forgetting the smile exists. The whole point of the learning objective is that the smile changes the Greeks.

d.reason: That delta is a first-order approximation is true and irrelevant here. The question asks about the direction of the adjustment, which the chain rule signs unambiguously. This is a hedged-sounding non-answer.

trap.explanation: The put half is where candidates fall: 'higher than $-0.40$' means a value like $-0.35$, not $-0.45$, and because put-call parity forces both deltas to shift by the same amount, a candidate who reasons that the put 'becomes more sensitive' has confused magnitude with signed value. A separate distractor simply omits the smile-adjustment term altogether, recovering the unadjusted BSM answer, and another hides behind a true but irrelevant caveat about delta being an approximation.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of the volatility smile on the CALCULATION of an option's Greek letter risk measures
questions.reading: Hull, Ch. 20: Volatility Smiles
questions.question: A call option is struck at USD 20.00 and is currently at the money, so that $d_1 = 0$ and the BSM delta is 0.50. Asset returns are not lognormal. Instead, the implied distribution has a LIGHT left tail and a HEAVY right tail. What happens to the TRUE delta of the call as the stock price rises toward USD 21.00, moving the option from at the money to slightly in the money?

options.text: Delta remains 0.50.
Delta rises above 0.50.
Delta falls below 0.50.
The net effect is indeterminate.

questions.solution:
This question shows that the two components of true delta can reinforce or oppose one another, and that under a reverse skew they oppose, so the net sign cannot be determined without magnitudes.

Apply the same decomposition as in the companion question and sign each term separately.

$$\text{true delta} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial S} + \text{vega} \times \frac{\partial \sigma_{imp}}{\partial S}$$

**Term 1: the standard BSM effect.** As the stock rises from USD 20.00 to USD 21.00 the call moves from at the money toward in the money, so $N(d_1)$ rises above 0.50. Term 1 is positive.

**Term 2: the smile effect.** A light left tail and a heavy right tail means implied volatility is an increasing function of $K/S(0)$. The strike is fixed at USD 20.00, so a rise in $S$ lowers $K/S(0)$, which therefore lowers implied volatility. Since vega is positive, term 2 is negative.

The two terms pull in opposite directions. Without knowing the steepness of the skew and the size of vega, the net effect on true delta cannot be signed. The answer is indeterminate.

Contrast with the two related cases, which complete the learning objective:

| Case | Term 1 | Term 2 | Net effect on true delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flat smile (no skew) | positive | zero (vega $\times$ 0) | Unambiguously the BSM direction |
| Standard equity skew | positive | positive | Unambiguously higher than BSM delta |
| Reverse skew (this item) | positive | negative | Indeterminate |

a.reason: Delta stays at 0.50 only if the underlying does not move at all. Here the stock rises by USD 1.00, so at minimum term 1 is active.

b.reason: This is the correct answer for the ordinary equity skew, where the two terms reinforce – the right mechanism applied to the wrong skew direction.

c.reason: This would require the smile effect to be both negative and larger in magnitude than the standard delta effect. Nothing in the stem establishes the relative magnitudes, so asserting this is an unwarranted claim.

d.reason: Opposing signs with unspecified magnitudes gives an indeterminate net effect.

trap.explanation: The trap targets anyone running on equity-skew autopilot who assumes the two terms always reinforce, when here they oppose because the skew runs the other way. The correct discipline is to write the two terms, sign each one separately, and only conclude a determinate direction when the signs agree; a further distractor asserts a determinate direction opposite to BSM without any basis for the relative magnitudes needed to establish it.
